title: Bara Masa, Tera Parba: osha, story and food
scope: Fifty-three selected profiles: fifteen narrative checkpoints and thirty-eight research notes. No claim of exhaustive coverage or completed history.

pages.name: Khudurukuni Osha
pages.traditional_month: Bhadraba
pages.lead: A small offering of rice carries a story of hunger, a sister’s hope and brothers away at sea.

sections.title: The story remembered
sections.text: In Deeti Ray’s account, Tapoi is the only sister of seven merchant brothers. During their absence, most of her sisters-in-law mistreat her. She encounters girls worshipping Mangala and offers the little khuda she has, asking for help. Her brothers return and discover her suffering. This is a ritual narrative, not a verified biography.
sections.locator: 2020 article, Tapoi narrative following the evening ritual

sections.title: Girls as keepers of the observance
sections.text: Ray describes Bhadraba Sundays in coastal Odisha: gathering flowers, a sand image called balunka, rice-paste decoration and evening recitation. Her photographs identify Pattamundai in Kendrapara as one setting. Girls organise and perform the worship. The account documents a particular cultural tradition; it does not establish identical practice in every district.
sections.locator: 2020 article, ritual sequence; Balunka caption

sections.title: Food makes the story tangible
sections.text: Patra’s 2019 essay identifies khuda as rice particles offered to Mangala. He connects the observance with a text attributed to Gopinath Das and with coastal maritime memory. The food association is stronger than any claim that a specific voyage occurred. Ray’s English food glosses sometimes use bran or husk; these are not interchangeable food-processing terms. We retain khuda and leave its preparation-specific identification for an Odia text and cook’s account.
sections.locator: Patra printed p.48; Ray food-offerings paragraph

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: An editorial reading of this story asks who receives care when a household’s earners are absent. The offering matters because of the giver’s circumstances. A food article can therefore follow rice through work, unequal access and devotion, rather than treating it only as a recipe. This interpretation should be tested against the words of present-day observers.

sections.title: History still to establish
sections.text: A twentieth- or twenty-first-century description is evidence that a tradition was recorded then, not its starting date. Manuscript and printed witnesses of the Tapoi text need to be compared before assigning a composition date. The 2022 journal paper has been located, but its original file was not recovered in this pass. Ray’s two publications would remain one author’s research lineage.
sections.locator: Publication and attribution boundaries

questions: How is khuda named and prepared in this locality?
Which Tapoi book or oral version is recited, and who taught it?
How have the worship group and food sharing changed?

pages.name: Manabasa Gurubara
pages.traditional_month: Margasira
pages.lead: A measure of grain becomes a way to think about sustenance, dignity and who may share a meal.

sections.title: Lakshmi and the rejected devotee
sections.text: Balabhadra Ghadai retells the Lakshmi Purana associated with Balaram Das: Lakshmi honours Sriya, a devotee identified in the narrative as Chandala. Balabhadra objects to the visit, and Jagannath excludes Lakshmi. The conflict centres on caste and the goddess’s freedom to recognise devotion. This is the text’s story, not evidence that discrimination subsequently disappeared.
sections.locator: Cult of Goddess Mahalakshmi, printed p.102

sections.title: Hunger changes the argument
sections.text: The Mohantys’ 2021 essay describes the brothers’ hardship after Lakshmi leaves and reads the work as a challenge to caste barriers. Food becomes central to the dispute over authority. Our interpretation is that a household’s feeding labour is made visible through its withdrawal: those who dismiss its source discover their dependence on it.
sections.locator: Printed p.23, Lakshmi Purana discussion

sections.title: The meal and the recognition
sections.text: In Ghadai’s retelling, the hungry brothers reach Lakshmi’s new household. Told that its mistress is Chandala, they first attempt to cook for themselves and fail. They finally accept her cooked food, recognise its familiar preparation and reunite with her. The reversal makes exclusion answerable to the experience of hunger. Ghadai himself says the story’s time of formation is not definitely known.
sections.locator: Printed pp.103–104

sections.title: The household observance
sections.text: The same essay places the worship on Margasira Thursdays and identifies the mana or grain measure among its objects. Dash records khiri, khechudi, kakara and chakuli as associated foods. These are attributed examples, not a compulsory menu for every Thursday or home.
sections.locator: Mohanty p.23; Dash p.17

sections.title: A history of text, voice and work
sections.text: The next historical step is to identify dated editions and manuscripts of Lakshmi Purana and compare how they are read aloud. The author attribution alone does not date today’s menu or decorations. The collection should credit the reader, cook and person who draws the household designs, including work that a dish photograph would leave invisible.

sections.title: A visitor’s starting point
sections.text: Learn the meaning of the grain measure and ask a willing cook about one preparation. A shop selling chakuli does not provide access to a household’s Manabasa worship. A future tasting record needs its own date, provider and consent.

questions: Which edition or inherited oral passage is used?
Which offerings differ across the Thursdays?
What does the family say about Sriya and shared food?

pages.name: Sudasa Brata
pages.lead: A knotted thread and an offering of manda connect a recurring vow with Lakshmi.

sections.title: The vow and its objects
sections.text: The Mohantys describe a thread with ten knots, each associated with a name of Lakshmi. Mahanti gives the calendrical condition as a Thursday coinciding with the bright fortnight’s tenth lunar day; it can recur within a year. Dash’s Kartika-only description is therefore retained as a conflict, not used as the general rule.
sections.locator: Mohanty p.25; Mahanti p.43; Dash p.15

sections.title: Manda in the offering
sections.text: Dash names manda for Sudasa. The existing food record describes a steamed version, but that does not establish the recipe of every ritual offering. The useful questions concern dough, filling, cooking method, number and distribution. A dish name can remain stable while its preparation varies.
sections.locator: Printed pp.17–18

sections.title: Two stories around the vow
sections.text: In the scanned verse booklet, a kite takes a Brahmin woman’s ritual thread and the king gives her the queen’s brata; Nala and Damayanti later endure hardship before renewal and restoration. In the typed prose, a cat steals a merchant wife’s manda and King Sudarshana obtains a replacement from Queen Sudasha’s offering. The merchant’s wife later helps the queen renew the vow. The thread and the cake carry different narrative roles. Neither story establishes a historical event.
sections.locator: Verse printed pp.1–12; prose PDF pp.1–4

sections.title: What history can and cannot say
sections.text: The sources connect the brata to Lakshmi devotion, but no earliest Odisha performance is established here. Mahanti’s claim of revival by Balarama Das still needs a dated textual witness. The two recovered copies tell different stories, so neither is treated as a single authoritative original.
sections.locator: Printed p.43

sections.title: Reading its significance
sections.text: A useful editorial lens is the relationship between an enduring object and repeated action: a thread can remind its wearer of a vow between observances. This is a question to explore with practitioners, not an assertion that everyone gives the thread the same meaning.

sections.title: A printed offering passage
sections.text: An undated verse booklet naming Damayanti in its title describes ten manda with chhena and coconut filling. Damayanti is a character in its story, not an established author credit. The passage supplies a textual food reference while leaving the cooking method unresolved; it does not prove the observance’s starting date or a recipe followed by every household.
sections.locator: Printed pp.2–3, especially verse17 on p.2; PDF p.3

sections.title: Manuscripts to compare
sections.text: The National Mission for Manuscripts lists five Sudasa Brata Katha accessions: ORPR-64, ORPR-210, ORPR-220, ORPR-221 and ORPR-226. Their texts and copying dates remain unexamined; separate catalogue entries do not yet establish separate narrative variants.
sections.locator: PDF pp.20–21

questions: Which dated colophons establish the transmission of each story?
How do the two stories circulate in different localities?
Is manda steamed or fried in each documented household version, and what dough is used?

pages.name: Dutiya Osha
pages.traditional_month: Ashwina
pages.lead: Dutiya’s food story begins before the curry is cooked. Produce is gathered for an offering, then becomes ghanta for a meal and exchange. Reading the occasion through that movement reveals women’s ritual work and relationships between households. Its stories and names need equally careful handling: a published Jimutavahana retelling, a coastal description and western Pua Jiuntia accounts are related reading, not one interchangeable history.

sections.title: Produce changes its role
sections.text: Pratap Kumar Dash’s2006 essay describes fruits and vegetables arranged as bhoga and used for ghanta the next day. Mahanti’s coastal account names twenty-one seasonal vegetables under an aparamanga leaf, later cooked and exchanged as ghanta tarkari. Dash names an Apamaranga branch elsewhere. A branch and a covering leaf are different descriptions; neither source here establishes the plant’s botanical identity. These accounts support a sequence of offering, cooking and sharing, rather than a compulsory ingredient list.
sections.locator: Dash printed15/PDF1 and17/PDF3; Mahanti printed58/PDF74

sections.title: A maternal vow and its figures
sections.text: Mahanti presents Dwitibabana as Surya’s son through a Brahmin widow and describes women praying for children’s long lives or hoping for a child. This is a belief account, not biological or historical evidence. He names sand figures of a fox and kite; Dash says fox and eagle. We retain those source words rather than assign one bird species. The complete local story explaining the figures has not been recovered.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed58/PDF74; Dash printed15/PDF1

sections.title: A published story of choosing to protect another
sections.text: Rajalakshmi Tripathy’s2023 essay retells Jimutavahana discovering the remains of snakes sacrificed to Garuda. He offers himself in a snake’s place; the arriving snake intervenes, and Jimutavahana persuades Garuda to renounce violence. The retelling ends with his marriage to Malayavati and her introduction of the vow. Tripathy calls it an Odia Ramayana story without identifying an edition or passage. We present her retelling, not an established founding event or the recovered fox-and-bird katha.
sections.locator: Published6October2023; narrative paragraphs, web27–28

sections.title: An offering list is not a recipe
sections.text: Dash’s food paragraph prints jambila, naranga, kerandakoli and padma puskar among Dutiya’s required fruits/items. These source forms remain unresolved here; we do not identify species or treat them as the complete curry. The adjacent list of Dudha gainthala, mula kanji, muga manda and muga paiti belongs to his discussion of Danda Panhara and must not be copied into Dutiya’s menu. A named household preparation, quantities and substitutions are still needed.
sections.locator: Printed17/PDF3, right column, Dutiya passage followed by Danda Panhara

sections.title: Compare western Odisha without erasing it
sections.text: The saved Pua Jiuntia study records Mahanti’s jugara and tikhiri offerings, followed by a vegetable curry, suji manda and kheeri. E Kiran Mohan’s Barpali account differs in vegetable count, wrapping leaf and thread placement. Those details remain on that regional page. Shared Dutibahana naming and a maternal vow invite comparison but do not establish that every coastal Dutiya household follows the same sequence, dishes or story.

sections.title: Where history still needs a text
sections.text: Saved institutional catalogue records identify Duti Bahana Osha at ORPR-106 and Dwitia Osha at OL-2452, and museum palm-leaf entries OL/2673 and OL/2674. Their contents and copying dates remain uninspected. The existing portal lead advertises a22-chapter Bruhat Dwitibahan Osha credited to Purusottam Das but offers an app-only route. Neither listing verifies authorship, edition date or earliest observance. Tripathy’s early-panji and Dhauli claims stay quarantined because no identified original passage has been recovered.
sections.locator: NMM PDF21,45; museum OL/2673,2674; Tripathy web26; existing text-witness portal lead

sections.title: Reading significance through food and care
sections.text: The offering-to-meal sequence gives this page its organising idea: ritual food becomes food exchanged between people. Mothers’ preparation and fasting make care visible in the published accounts; exchange makes the occasion larger than an individual plate. This is an editorial reading of documented actions, not a measured social, nutritional or economic effect. The wish for children’s protection stays within the observers’ belief.

sections.title: A seasonal enquiry, not a promised meal
sections.text: Mahanti gives Ashwina’s dark eighth, while the saved register retains Tripathy’s seventh-day statement as a conflict. No annual date is generated. Odisha Tourism also describes ghanta in a general Jajpur food listing; that does not establish a Dutiya meal or an operating venue. A visitor enquiry should identify the preparation, confirmed date, provider and welcome separately. Private worship and shared household food do not themselves establish visitor access.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed58/PDF74; retained text-witness calendar conflict; Tourism gastronomy heading

questions: Recover an identified local fox-and-bird katha and collate ORPR-106, OL-2452, OL/2673 and OL/2674 before claiming story identity or chronology.
Identify Tripathy’s cited Odia Ramayana and early panji editions; retain Dhauli claim quarantine until an exact inscription supports it.
Identify the named plant and offering items from a sourced botanical/local account; separate leaves, branches, fruits and curry ingredients.
Document an attributed household ghanta, sharing recipients and regional sequence; confirm local panji before annual-date advice.

pages.name: Budhei Osha
pages.traditional_month: Bhadraba
pages.lead: Budhei brings a kitchen’s grinding stones into worship. Across successive Wednesdays, a coconut is kept for the final offering and chapters are read aloud. This creates a food story about waiting and return: familiar objects and ingredients acquire a new role within the household. Published accounts name different deities and different calendar boundaries; those differences belong in the story.

sections.title: The kitchen stone becomes a ritual figure
sections.text: Mahanti describes women worshipping sila and silapua, bathed with turmeric or aonla water, marked with vermilion and collyrium and wrapped in a red sari. He glosses the pair as mortar and pestle; the local report uses the Odia names. We retain sila and silapua rather than silently turn the objects into a single standardized kitchen implement. Their everyday food work invites an editorial connection to preparation, but does not establish the observance’s historical origin.
sections.locator: Printed56–57/PDF72–73

sections.title: Names do not settle one deity
sections.text: Dash names Bimala or Tarini; Mahanti gives Mangala with Bamana as Jagannatha and also records a feminine Budha-graha identification. These are attributed explanations, not proof that all communities mean the same deity or that Budhei, Sudhei and Budhibaman are universally interchangeable. Mahanti distinguishes this Bhadraba observance from year-round Wednesday Budha worship.
sections.locator: Dash printed15/PDF1; Mahanti printed56–57/PDF72–73

sections.title: The coconut carries the month
sections.text: Mahanti says the first Wednesday’s coconut is broken and offered on the last; fruit and unspecified pitha accompany worship, and one katha chapter is read each Wednesday. That gives a sequence rather than a one-day menu. The object kept from one week to another ties preparation to anticipation. The latter is our editorial reading, not a measured social effect.
sections.locator: Printed57/PDF73

sections.title: A Bolagarh report names the foods
sections.text: Pradhan’s27September2023 report lists coconut, banana, fruits, muan, ukhuda, khai and kakara as offerings. It describes the retained coconut being used in pitha on the final Wednesday and at least five pitha/pana types for the closing observance. It does not identify all five preparations or quantities. Kakara is a named association here; its general preparation versions do not establish this household’s recipe.
sections.locator: Report food paragraphs, web29,31

sections.title: A published summary points toward several stories
sections.text: Puriwaves summarizes a wine dealer’s wife and a pregnant Brahmin woman receiving divine help. It also names a Magadha merchant couple, a Sundhi couple of Jajatinagara and Bandhu Mohanti of Jajpur as story strands. These are this website’s attributed myth summaries, including healing beliefs; they are neither historical events nor medical claims. The complete episodes and their relationship to successive readings remain unverified.
sections.locator: Myth-summary paragraph, web19

sections.title: Where a history must begin
sections.text: Institutional records list OL-2022, OL-2443 and palm-leaf OL/2636. Their catalogued extents differ, but that does not establish independent variants, composition dates or an earliest observance. Banamalli’s book route returned403. The recovered OdiaPortal page offers an app link rather than an inspected text. A locked Pratilipi series is another lead; no author attribution is transferred to the older katha.
sections.locator: NMM PDF13,45; museum OL/2636; portal app link

sections.title: Significance in repetition and care
sections.text: The repeated reading and first-to-last coconut make time visible through household actions. The saved accounts frame worship around hopes for children and their wellbeing. We can narrate those hopes respectfully while keeping reported beliefs distinct from effects. A fuller story needs a particular reader, locality, text and preparation; no interviews or local review have yet supplied them.

sections.title: Use the season as an enquiry
sections.text: Mahanti gives Bhadraba Wednesdays. Pradhan reports four or five observances and differing Gamha-Purnima or sankranti boundaries. No universal count or Gregorian date follows. The report’s fasting account is descriptive, not a visitor instruction. Confirm the local calendar and a publicly offered preparation separately; household worship and a named food do not establish a serving venue or invitation.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed56–57; report web30–31

questions: Collate original OL-2022, OL-2443 and OL/2636 episodes, copying dates and author/edition evidence; retry accessible text routes17October.
Distinguish local Budhei/Sudhei/Budhibaman deity names and the relation of merchant, Sundhi, Brahmin and Bandhu Mohanti episodes.
Document a named final-Wednesday menu and Kakara/coconut-pitha preparation without assuming a universal set of five.
Confirm local lunar or solar boundaries and consent for any visitor encounter; no annual date or venue established.

pages.name: Alana Osha
pages.traditional_month: Ashwina in Dash and Mahanti; Dhanu solar Sundays in a modern collected retelling (unresolved)
pages.lead: Alana makes restraint part of food culture. Its saved descriptions discuss salt, while a modern story begins with daughters excluded from a pitha meal. These are different kinds of evidence: an account of observance and a narrated explanation. Their calendars also disagree.

sections.title: What does without salt mean?
sections.text: Dash says that no salt is eaten during Alana; Mahanti says no salt is added to the bhoga, generally fruits and sweets. The first wording concerns consumption, the second preparation of offerings. They do not establish identical restrictions, their duration or a household menu. Dash’s adjacent general rice-and-biri cakes and khiri discussion is not an Alana recipe.
sections.locator: Dash printed17/PDF3; Mahanti printed58/PDF74

sections.title: Keep the deities and calendars attributed
sections.text: Dash lists Ashwina and Lakshmi. Mahanti describes Ashwina, Surya and married women. Shrutilipi’s collected account instead gives sunrise worship on Dhanu Sundays ending at Makar Sankranti. Solar Dhanu is not silently converted into lunar Pausa. The differences remain unresolved; one season or deity cannot yet be presented as universal.
sections.locator: Dash printed15/PDF1; Mahanti printed58/PDF74; Shrutilipi paragraph2

sections.title: Two daughters and a pitha meal
sections.text: In Shrutilipi’s retelling, a Chakulia Panda abandons his daughters after their mother shares rice-and-biri pitha with them. A protector shelters them. They learn Alana using materials left by celestial women, including banana peel and coconut. Prosperity follows; after marriages, the elder daughter loses wealth when she neglects the observance. These are narrative events and beliefs, not verified history.
sections.locator: Chapter245 paragraphs2–5

sections.title: Food in a story is not an offering recipe
sections.text: The story’s opening pitha is a disputed family meal. It does not establish an Alana offering, a named pitha variety, salt content or preparation method. Mahanti’s fruits and sweets are the documented offering categories; no particular sweet, quantity or serving venue is verified.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed58/PDF74; chapter245 paragraphs3,5

sections.title: Significance: exclusion, care and remembrance
sections.text: Our editorial reading asks who may share a meal and who is denied it. The mother’s sharing and the protector’s care contrast with the father’s exclusion. The vow becomes a way of remembering help after circumstances improve. This interpretation belongs to the inspected modern story; it does not prove how all observers understand Alana.

sections.title: A modern witness is not an origin date
sections.text: The listing dates this collected retelling26December2025 and names no original author. We have inspected its complete short narrative, not an older verse edition or manuscript. Its relationship to other two-sister stories remains uncollated. No earliest observance, regional distribution, author attribution or independent variant is established.
sections.locator: Listing date/credit; chapter245

sections.title: A seasonal visitor enquiry remains open
sections.text: The calendar conflict prevents a reliable single-season recommendation. A named association does not confirm a public meal, access to household worship or host consent. Before a visitor guide offers a date or preparation, verify a situated calendar and a separately advertised public food offer. Alana, Kanji Anla and Anla Navami remain distinct research identities.

Resolve Ashwina/Lakshmi, Ashwina/Surya and Dhanu Sunday accounts by locality, text and calendar; do not harmonise solar and lunar labels.
Document whether salt restraint applies to offerings, meals or both, its duration and actual local preparations.

pages.name: Kanji Anla Osha
pages.traditional_month: Margasira
pages.lead: Kanji Anla brings a sour rice-water preparation into worship of Sasthi. Its food, household story and calendar need to be read together, with room for differences between accounts.

sections.title: A mother’s appeal to Sasthi
sections.text: In Mahakud’s 2021 retelling, a merchant’s pregnant daughter-in-law takes a neighbour’s pumpkin. A curse is followed by the disappearance of her children and expulsion from her home. Alone in a forest, she appeals to Sasthi, who returns the children and instructs the vow. This is a modern devotional retelling without an identified old edition; it does not establish historical events or the observance’s date of origin.
sections.locator: Two story paragraphs preceding the ritual-procedure heading

sections.title: What the story asks us to notice
sections.text: The narrative joins forbidden taking, maternal distress, household rejection and restoration. That is an editorial reading of this retelling, not a claim about every observer’s interpretation. The blame placed on the mother belongs to the story’s conflict; it is not evidence that a mother causes a child’s misfortune. A merchant household in a devotional story also cannot establish a historical voyage or trade route.

sections.title: The offering and the ritual object
sections.text: Mahanti describes worship of Sasthi with seven dried fish dressed in yellow cloth, and offerings of kanji, aonla and sukua. Food offered for eating and fish arranged as ritual figures need to be recorded as different roles. His account supports neither a blanket vegetarian description of all osha offerings nor a claim that every household follows this practice.
sections.locator: Printed p.60 / PDF76

sections.title: A kitchen figure and a courtyard arrangement
sections.text: Sarangi describes a dried-fish figure dressed as a bride, seated on a stool in a kitchen corner beside kanji and dried-fish rai. Mahakud describes evening worship near the tulasi platform, a small water-filled pit and seven dressed fish figures. These are author-specific descriptions with no identified fieldwork locality. Their different settings should remain visible rather than be combined into one ritual sequence.
sections.locator: Sarangi Kanji Anla passage / web172; Mahakud ritual-procedure paragraph / web88

sections.title: After the offering: children and separate ritual materials
sections.text: Mahakud lists rice, dal, kanji, a taro–radish–dried-fish curry and two chakuli pithas. He describes feeding the offerings to the children for whom the vow was made, then burying or immersing the remainder. Poi stalks placed beside the fish figures have a separate non-sharing rule in his account. This is an attributed description, not a disposal instruction or a claim about every household.
sections.locator: Ritual-procedure paragraph / web88

sections.title: Care expressed through a meal
sections.text: Read alongside the mother’s appeal in the story, feeding the intended children gives the offering a concrete relationship: the household’s hope is expressed through preparing and sharing food. This is an editorial interpretation of the published retelling. It does not establish an observed benefit, a universal meaning or permission to enter private worship.

sections.title: Kanji in two written descriptions
sections.text: Dash defines kanji with broken rice, radish, sour rice-water and curry leaves. Sarangi describes vegetables including radish, papaya and pumpkin cooked in pakhala liquid, then tempered with dry chilli, panchphutana and curry leaves; dried-fish rai is a separate preparation. These accounts describe related food practices, not one standardized ingredient list.
sections.locator: Dash printed p.18 note2 / PDF4; Sarangi Prathamastami–Kanji Anla paragraph

sections.title: Why the day stays unresolved
sections.text: Mahanti places the observance towards evening on Prathamastami. Sarangi places it the following day; Mahakud names Margasira’s dark ninth. We retain the disagreement rather than assign a universal calendar rule. A locality-specific annual notice and an inspected katha edition are still needed; no Gregorian date is confirmed.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed p.60 / PDF76; Sarangi Kanji Anla passage; Mahakud opening calendar paragraph

sections.title: Culinary knowledge and the science still to test
sections.text: The accounts document sour rice-water use, cooking and tempering. They do not measure fermentation time, temperature, acidity, organisms or survival after cooking. We can describe the practical knowledge without claiming a probiotic benefit. Health explanations in the modern retelling remain unsupported by an inspected experimental study. A future preparation record should document ingredients, vessel, water source, timing and subsequent heating before any food-science conclusion.

sections.title: Names that should stay distinct
sections.text: Kanji Anla remains a separate observance from Alana and Anla Navami. Sarangi discusses Anla Navami in a Kartika passage and Kanji Anla after Prathamastami in Margasira. Similar spelling and a shared food vocabulary do not prove that these are interchangeable names.
sections.locator: Kartika Anla Navami passage / web161; Prathamastami–Kanji Anla passage / web172

sections.title: Comparing everyday food without promising a visit
sections.text: Our torani-kanji food entry is a useful comparison for rice-water cooking. Its modern household recipe is not the ritual recipe established here. A Margasira food association can help a visitor ask informed questions, but this research identifies no serving venue, public distribution, invitation to private worship or current availability.
