pages.name: Ananta Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava in Mahanti; Ashwina in Dash (unresolved)
pages.lead: Ananta Brata makes a long commitment tangible through a knotted thread, counted offerings and a story heard together. Food is part of both the worship and the sharing that follows.

sections.title: An Odisha account, with a calendar question
sections.text: Mahanti describes married women observing a fourteen-year vow for the welfare of husbands and children, dedicated to Vishnu on Bhadrava shukla Chaturdashi. Dash’s inventory instead places Ananta in Ashwina and names Ananta murti or Basuki. These descriptions remain separate: a differing month or dedication cannot be explained away as a regional variant without locality evidence. No annual Gregorian date has been assigned.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed46–47 / PDF62–63; Dash printed16 / PDF2

sections.title: Fourteen puris and fourteen manda pithas
sections.text: Mahanti describes a fast, fourteen sindur dots on a wooden plank, and fourteen puris with fourteen manda pithas as bhoga. A bowl of panchamruta represents the ocean of milk. His footnote34 specifies milk, honey, ghee, curd and jaggery. A fourteen-knotted thread is wrapped around a cucumber and swirled five times in this mixture. An elderly woman reads the katha, the family listens, and the offerings are shared with relatives and friends. Neither the manda filling nor its cooking method is given. The cucumber has a stated ritual role; its later consumption is not established.
sections.locator: Printed46–47 / PDF62–63, footnote34

sections.title: A Sanskrit story witness
sections.text: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva94, places the vow in bright-fortnight Bhadrapada. Sheila learns it from women beside a river after marrying Kaundinya. Prosperity follows; her husband angrily breaks her thread, and the household loses its wealth. His search ends in Ananta’s appearance and a renewed fourteen-year commitment. This is a ritual narrative, not verified biography. The inspected digital Sanskrit chapter does not establish when the observance reached Odisha.

sections.title: Why the retellings cannot be blended
sections.text: The Kamakoti synopsis makes Sheila herself discard the thread and has her husband caution her. The SanskritDocuments manual instead has Kaundinya burn it and Susheela rescue it in milk. The Sanskrit chapter’s verse40 describes an angry breaking of the thread; it does not supply the manual’s burning-and-milk scene there. These are documented differences among displayed texts. We have not established independent oral traditions, their relationships, or which version a particular Odisha household recites.
sections.locator: Kamakoti chapter34 Ananta section; manual section47; Sanskrit chapter94 verse40

sections.title: Food prescriptions travel with texts
sections.text: Agni Purana192 describes rice-flour pupa divided between a Brahmin recipient and the observer, along with worship and a consecrated thread. The selected verses do not name an Odisha dish or give a local recipe. The modern SanskritDocuments manual calls its offering Atiras and specifies twenty-eight; we do not silently rename that food Odia arisa or substitute it for Mahanti’s manda and puris. A textual prescription, an Odisha descriptive account and a named household’s preparation are distinct evidence.
sections.locator: Agni192 verses7–11; manual section47 food prescription

sections.title: Knowledge carried by repetition
sections.text: As an editorial interpretation, counting offerings, tying knots, renewing a vow and hearing a story together create a memorable structure for passing on practice. The cooking work also deserves study: dough preparation, shaping, heat control, ingredient choice and sharing. The current account does not document those techniques closely enough to reconstruct a recipe or claim a scientific explanation. Nor do narrative promises demonstrate medical benefits or a measured link between ritual and prosperity.

sections.title: Reading the season respectfully
sections.text: Ananta offers a reason to explore manda and household food traditions, but ritual association does not guarantee that a restaurant serves the food or that a family welcomes visitors. No host, public event, annual date or current serving venue is verified here. A complete identified Odia katha, local accounts and dated historical records are the next steps.

pages.name: Rabinarayana Brata
pages.traditional_month: Sunday–Ekadashi rule; Margasira in Dash, unresolved
pages.lead: Rabinarayana Brata brings the sun, the lunar calendar and everyday materials into one act of devotion. Its offerings show why food culture includes more than a list of dishes: fruit, grain and prepared sweets can have different ritual roles.

sections.title: A weekday meets a lunar day
sections.text: Mahanti describes the observance when Ekadashi falls on Sunday and identifies the deity as Surya. His passage does not specify the fortnight or restrict the month. Dash instead lists Rabinarayan in Margasira and separately lists Pusa Rabibara in Pausa. Those entries should not be merged into one Sunday festival. The calendar descriptions remain unresolved; we have not assigned a Gregorian date.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 44–45 / PDF 60–61; Dash printed 16 / PDF 2

sections.title: Materials counted in sevens
sections.text: Mahanti describes women wearing a ritual thread containing seven blades of duba grass, seven barakoli leaves and seven raw rice grains, tied with seven folds of thread. After bathing they offer water to Surya and worship with seven kinds of flowers and seven kinds of fruit. The rice here is part of the thread assembly, not a documented cooked offering or meal. The fruit species, sharing practice and food eaten afterwards are unspecified.
sections.locator: Printed 45 / PDF 61, Rabinarayana entry

sections.title: Mua and manda in an Odia account
sections.text: Bishnumohan Adhikari’s 2020 account on Antaranga Kalinga specifies bright-fortnight Ekadashi on Sunday. It names seven mua and seven manda among the offerings, alongside flowers and durba, and describes a seven-knotted thread and water offering. This is an attributed cultural description; it gives no recipe, filling, grain variety or preparation method. We therefore keep its prepared-food names beside Mahanti’s fruit account without combining them into a mandatory menu.
sections.locator: Calendar paragraph and final offering paragraph

sections.title: The story has identifiable textual leads
sections.text: Mahanti says the Rabinarayana brata katha is read but does not recount it. The National Mission for Manuscripts’ Odisha State Museum catalogue lists Rabinarayana Brata under ORPR-218 and ORPR-236, and a combined Rabi Narayana Brata Katha, Kanchi Kaberi record under CY-1847,1848. These are three catalogue records, not three established versions of the story. The listed extents cannot supply a date of composition, author or plot, and the combined record’s extent is not the length of the brata alone.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 45 / PDF 61; catalogue PDF 21 and 55

sections.title: Hope, memory and the work of observance
sections.text: Mahanti associates the vow with women’s hopes for children. That describes a devotional intention, not evidence of fertility treatment. As an editorial reading, repeated counting and assembling plant materials may offer a useful way to explore how practice is remembered and taught. The calendar rule also invites research into who consults an almanac and how dates are settled locally. Neither detail establishes a particular astronomical calculation, an ancient scientific theory or an explanation for the number seven.

sections.title: Keeping related solar observances distinct
sections.text: The separate Rabibara paragraph in Mahanti describes Sunday fasting, an evening meal and almsgiving. Those details are not explicitly attached to Rabinarayana in its own entry. Likewise, Samba Dashami’s story and named dishes belong to that observance’s sources. Sharing a solar dedication does not establish an identical narrative, date or menu.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 63 / PDF 79, separate Rabibara entry; Dash printed 16 / PDF 2

sections.title: For seasonal food exploration
sections.text: Manda and mua are useful names to ask about, with the source limitations kept visible. No current serving venue, consenting household host, annual event or visit date is verified. The full identified Odia text and accounts from named localities are needed before a complete narrative or practical food itinerary can be offered.

pages.name: Somnath Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava to Aswina; culmination on shukla dashami
pages.lead: Somnath Brata brings together a sacred thread, pitha offerings and the telling of a story. Its surviving accounts offer a way to explore how food preparation and listening carry a vow through household life.

sections.title: A vow across two months
sections.text: Mahanti describes a period from Bhadrava shukla sasthi to Aswina shukla dashami, identified as Vijaya Dashami. Shiva and Parbati are worshipped, mainly by women seeking family well-being. Dash’s shorter inventory places Somanath in Bhadrab and lists Kukkuti separately. These are descriptions of customary timing; no annual visitor date has been verified.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 48–49 / PDF 64–65; Dash printed 15 / PDF 1

sections.title: The king, the queen and the neglected vow
sections.text: In the recovered Odia copy, Shiva tells Parvati about King Birabikrama and Somnath’s visiting ascetics. The king welcomes and feeds them but rejects their invitation to observe the vow, fearing ridicule. A curse brings illness and loss. His queen, later displaced from the palace, learns the vow through women in a Brahmin settlement and obtains the ritual thread with a maid’s help. Her observance precedes his recovery and their reunion. This is the story’s devotional explanation, not historical biography or evidence that observance cures illness.
sections.locator: PDF pp.1–3; modern typed copy, edition undated

sections.title: What the offerings actually say
sections.text: Mahanti specifies ten types of pitha without naming them. The Odia copy instead calls for ten pithas with ten kinds of filling; ingredients and cooking method are unspecified. Its palace hospitality scene is a narrative meal, not a prescription for the ritual offering. The copy names Aswina shukla dashami for the vow. These details do not establish a standard manda recipe.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 49 / PDF 65; Odia copy PDF p.1 hospitality and calendar, pp.2–3 ritual directions

sections.title: Thread, gathering and sharing
sections.text: Mahanti describes ten strands and ten knots, names of Shiva recited while knotting, a midday gathering around a clay linga, an elderly woman reading the katha, and participants wearing the thread and sharing bhoga. He places Kukkuti on Somnath’s second day. Its separate identity must be researched before transferring this food account to it.
sections.locator: Printed 48–49 / PDF 64–65

sections.title: A literary history with a date still to test
sections.text: Subrat Kumar Prusty’s March 2014 Odisha Review article places Somanatha Brata Katha among early Odia prose texts and assigns it to the thirteenth century. His excerpt has Shiva addressing Parvati and introduces Malaba, Patala and King Birabikrama. It cites Kunja Bihari Tripathy’s Prachina Odia Gadya Sankalan (Odisha Sahitya Akademy, 1982), p.92. This is an attributed literary dating. The cited edition and its dating argument remain unread; neither the modern copy nor this excerpt establishes when the observance began. Similar opening characters do not establish textual identity.
sections.locator: Printed 10 / PDF 7; cited original not inspected

sections.title: Eight catalogue leads, not eight proven versions
sections.text: The National Mission for Manuscripts’ museum catalogue supplies eight selected Somanatha title records. One combines several works, and its manuscript identifier is reused for a different title in the next row. Accession, title and page location therefore remain essential. The records have not been collated or read as manuscripts; their extents, dates, authors and relationship to the recovered typed copy must not be inferred.
sections.locator: PDF 15,21,23,24,53; selected rows detailed in the text-witness register

sections.title: Significance and practical knowledge
sections.text: An editorial reading can follow the contrast between royal pride and the queen’s learning through other women. The preparations also raise questions about how people remember counts, teach knotting, vary fillings and coordinate a gathering. These are promising subjects for household research, not evidence of a particular ancient scientific theory. The numerical pattern alone does not explain why ten was chosen.

sections.text: Ask about locally named pithas and the distinction between offerings and food shared afterwards. A household vow does not establish a public food event. No consenting host, serving venue, access arrangement or current availability is verified; the guide records a cultural association only.

pages.name: Kukkuti Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava; exact local rule requires confirmation
pages.lead: Kukkuti Brata opens a path from Odisha’s household calendar to a wider textual tradition. The evidence is uneven: its name and dedication are locally documented, while the recovered story and food directions come from a Sanskrit comparator.

sections.title: Its place in Odisha’s calendar
sections.text: Pratap Kumar Dash lists Kukkuti in Bhadrab, dedicated to Shiva and Parvati. Mahanti places it on the second day of Somnath Brata, whose start he gives as Bhadrava shukla sasthi. This suggests a connection with the next lunar day, but the relative wording alone should not be converted into a verified annual date. Neither passage supplies a separate Kukkuti menu.
sections.locator: Dash printed15 / PDF1; Mahanti printed48–49 / PDF64–65

sections.title: Lalita Saptami: a textual comparison
sections.text: The Shabdakalpadruma entry for Lalitasaptami names Kukkuti and specifies Bhadra shukla saptami. Its directions include Shiva–Parvati worship, an eight-knotted thread wetted with milk, and eight fruits. This is a Sanskrit textual prescription, not verification of Odisha household practice or a universal alias in every locality.
sections.locator: Vol.4, displayed p.209, opening and directions before the narrative

sections.title: Friendship, forgetting and renewal
sections.text: In that entry’s story, Queen Chandramukhi and her friend Mala learn a vow from women by the Sarayu. Neglect is followed by rebirth as a monkey and a hen, then as Ishvari and Bhushana. Bereavement turns Ishvari’s friendship into jealousy; Bhushana offers to share the vow’s merit and explains its practice. The text frames this as consolation to Devaki. These are devotional narrative events, not a verified Odisha history or an explanation of real bereavement.
sections.locator: Vol.4 pp.209–210, narrative attributed there to Bhavishya Purana

sections.title: Food terms without an invented recipe
sections.text: The closing directions name payasa and pishtaka and place feeding kin before one’s own meal. They do not identify ingredients, cooking techniques or an Odisha dish. Milk’s use on the thread is distinct from a drink or meal. Somnath’s ten-pitha account cannot fill the missing local evidence.
sections.locator: Shabdakalpadruma p.209, closing food lines before p.210; Mahanti p.49

sections.title: A local manuscript lead to investigate
sections.text: A mirrored catalogue of the Orissa State Museum’s Smrti collection lists Kukkuti among four subjects in item148, a twelve-folio palm-leaf Vratakatha described as written in Oriya script. It supplies no copying date, findspot or colophon. The accession suffix is unclear in OCR and the page image could not be inspected. Twelve folia describe the combined record, not Kukkuti alone; Oriya script does not establish that the text is in the Odia language.
sections.locator: Printed85 / viewer139, item148; preface viewer9 identifies museum collection

sections.title: Comparative witnesses outside Odisha
sections.text: IGNCA’s catalogue provides four selected Kukkuti records from Saraswati Bhawan Library, Varanasi, in Sanskrit and Bangla script. One is described as incomplete and three as complete. Those labels describe catalogue assessments; the manuscripts themselves remain unread. Their titles establish research leads, not four independent versions, an Odisha origin or a proven route of transmission.

sections.title: What remains to understand
sections.text: The story invites an editorial inquiry into friendship, grief and the transmission of ritual knowledge among women. A local study could ask how the thread is made, who tells the story, which food terms people use and how preparation is learned. The text’s supernatural rewards and punishments are not evidence about health, fertility or parental responsibility. A dated original, an identified Odia telling and locality-specific accounts are still needed.

pages.name: Santoshi Mata Brata
pages.traditional_month: No fixed month; a sequence of Fridays
pages.lead: Santoshi Mata Brata gives the food calendar a weekly rhythm. Its small offering, fasting discipline and concluding meal have different roles; understanding those roles matters more than assigning it an invented annual season.

sections.title: A Friday vow in Odisha
sections.text: Mahanti describes a comparatively recent practice in Odisha, undertaken by men and women. It may begin at any time of year and continue for sixteen Fridays or until the vow is fulfilled; he also calls it Shola Shukrabara brata. His description supplies no arrival date. Dash’s 2006 inventory likewise identifies Friday fasting and avoidance of pickle. These are published descriptions, not a survey of current households.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed109–110 / PDF125–126; Dash printed15 / PDF1

sections.title: History: devotion before the film
sections.text: Philip Lutgendorf’s study says the Friday vow had spread in northern India for more than a decade before the 1975 film Jai Santoshi Maa. Cinema amplified an existing devotion. That history does not date its arrival in Odisha.
sections.locator: Printed24 / PDF1; film citation printed37 / PDF14; issue period July–August2002

sections.title: A story of separation and return
sections.text: In the pamphlet story summarised by Lutgendorf, a mistreated wife learns the vow from other women. Her absent husband returns, but relatives introduce sour food into the concluding feast. A repeated observance restores the household; the wife later recognises the goddess in frightening form. This is devotional narrative, not historical or causal evidence.
sections.locator: Printed25–26 / PDF2–3; note9 on printed36 credits Simha and Agnihotri2000 pp338–339

sections.title: Offering, abstention and completion
sections.text: Mahanti identifies gur-chana as raw sugar candy with roasted chickpea. He describes fasting, avoidance of eating or touching sour or bitter things, and an udyapana in which eight children are fed and given clothes and money. He does not give that meal’s dishes. The offering is therefore not a complete menu. His sugar terminology is retained without silently replacing it with a particular modern product.
sections.locator: Printed109–110 / PDF125–126

sections.title: A comparison that preserves differences
sections.text: Lutgendorf describes one meal during the fast and an ending feast for eight boys. Mahanti says eight children. Those formulations should remain attributed until local accounts clarify practice. The comparative source does not establish an Odisha completion-meal recipe.
sections.locator: Lutgendorf printed25 / PDF2; Mahanti printed110 / PDF126

sections.title: What food can help us understand
sections.text: An editorial reading can follow how a modest offering becomes a shared act of devotion, and how a meal marks completion of a promise. Future research should ask who obtains ingredients, prepares the meal, tells the story and teaches the rules. Roasting is a named preparation, but temperature, equipment and local technique remain undocumented here. Religious abstention does not by itself establish a nutritional or medical benefit.

sections.title: The missing Odia text
sections.text: An Odiabook listing points to an Odia Santoshi Maa Brata Katha associated with Shri Sarada Store and described as thirty-three pages. The linked book could not be retrieved. Its edition, author, narrative and food directions remain unread. The listing’s March2023 date is not evidence of when the book or observance originated.

pages.name: Kedar Brata
pages.traditional_month: Kartika
pages.lead: Kedar Brata brings together loss, recovery and carefully counted ritual materials. A recovered Odia telling makes its story readable, while the date of that telling and the details of present-day household meals remain open.

sections.title: Its place in the calendar
sections.text: Mahanti places Kedara Brata on Kartika purnima and describes worship of Kedarnath, identified as Shiva, with twenty-one wild flowers and twenty-one gua or betel nuts. Dash gives the same two counted offerings. These accounts establish published descriptions, not a current statewide survey or a public event date. The shared wording is not treated as proven independent corroboration.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed52 / PDF68; Dash printed15 / PDF1

sections.title: Kunti and the two sisters
sections.text: The Odia telling begins with Kunti grieving her family’s lost kingdom. A sage recommends the vow and recounts two impoverished sisters who learn it from celestial women. Prosperity follows; discarding the sacred thread brings another reversal, and renewed observance restores fortune. The frame closes with Kunti performing the vow. This is a devotional account of loss and renewal, not historical evidence of those events.
sections.locator: PDF2 frame; PDF4–9 sisters’ story; PDF9–11 Kunti’s observance and conclusion

sections.title: Food inside the telling
sections.text: The directions and narrative name banana, coconut and sugarcane, along with gua and other ritual materials. Prasad is received after worship. The repeated number twenty-one also organises thread and offerings; it is not a portion size or recipe. No cooking method is supplied for the three named foods.
sections.locator: PDF3 ritual directions; PDF5 and7 narrative offerings; PDF9–10 concluding preparation

sections.title: A textual witness with an unresolved date
sections.text: Project Pothi’s eleven-page file contains a digital cover and the Odia narrative. Its repository attributes scanning to Prateek Pattanaik and labels the author unknown. The repository’s seventeenth-century description and 2August1917 publication date are not confirmed by an original imprint in the inspected pages. They remain leads, not established chronology.
sections.locator: PDF1–11; Commons Summary, author/publication fields and file history

sections.title: The limits of historical evidence
sections.text: An indexed 1937 Orissa Gazette entry appears to describe another Kedara Brata booklet, attributed to Purushottama Das, with wording about Lakshmi. The original Gazette could not be fetched. That lead needs its page image and booklet identity checked before it can be joined to this Shiva narrative or used to date the tradition. A shared title alone cannot establish the same text.

sections.title: Significance and food culture
sections.text: An editorial reading follows how the story connects material insecurity with learning, remembering and renewing a vow. Counting flowers, nuts and thread can be studied as a practice of ritual preparation without claiming a hidden mathematical theory. Food research should distinguish an offering from what participants actually eat, and ask how households choose, obtain and distribute it. The story’s rewards do not establish real-world causes of poverty or prosperity.

sections.title: For visitors
sections.text: Kartika is a cultural browsing cue. The evidence does not establish a special dish sold in that season, a public meal, a consenting household host or current access. A visitor-facing food recommendation needs a separately verified serving place and date.

gua / betel nuts — counted ritual offering; consumption not established

pages.name: Rai Damodara Brata
pages.traditional_month: Kartika; precise start rule unresolved
pages.lead: Rai Damodara Brata connects the ritual year with the everyday work of eating: choosing ingredients, preparing a restrained meal and receiving temple food. Its story also brings the household world into Jagannath devotion.

sections.title: A name within the Kartika cycle
sections.text: Mahanti groups Kartika and Rai Damodara under one heading. He describes month-long observance, especially by widows, and a five-day panchuka option. Dash places Rai Damodara in Kartika. This supports a shared research entry, not the claim that every Kartika practice is identical.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed51–52 / PDF67–68; Dash printed16 / PDF2

sections.title: Rai and Lakshmi: the remembered story
sections.text: Mahanti recounts a legend in which Rai, a Puri servitor’s daughter, marries Jagannath. Lakshmi grants that Rai will be worshipped alongside her. This explains the name within that telling; it is neither a dated marriage record nor evidence of the observance’s historical beginning.
sections.locator: Printed51 / PDF67

sections.title: Food during the vow
sections.text: Mahanti describes habishanna or Mahaprasad eaten once daily. These are reported alternatives; he supplies no recipe. The distinction matters: a meal associated with a vow and food received after temple offering have different ritual roles.
sections.locator: Printed52 / PDF68

sections.title: A described Habisha Dalma
sections.text: Visit Bhubaneswar describes unroasted moong cooked without turmeric, with restricted vegetables including elephant apple and raw banana, and pepper in place of chilli. This is one attributed preparation. The previously saved 2019 chef-menu account is a separate contemporary context, not proof of household or temple uniformity.
sections.locator: Dalma section, Habisha paragraphs; chef context linked through Dalma page

sections.title: History and the limits of textual prescriptions
sections.text: Patra and Punit’s 2018 study interprets Kartika devotion through Puranic texts and widowhood. Its panchaka discussion describes arua rice and vegetables, with milk and curd on specified days. The underlying passages remain uninspected here. Prescriptive texts illuminate religious ideals but cannot establish what every participant ate or an uninterrupted Odisha chronology.
sections.locator: Printed34,36,38 / PDF2,4,6; note30 cites Skanda2.4.32.47,50–51

sections.title: Two calendar questions remain open
sections.text: Mahanti’s printed25 says the month-long vow starts on Kartika purnima, whereas printed51–52 describes the whole month and its final five days. The discrepancy is retained. Patra and Punit distinguish a month-long vow from a separate five-day vow on textual grounds. A local account must clarify which observance is meant before an annual date is assigned.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed25,51–52; Patra and Punit printed36 and38 note28

sections.title: Significance: a season made through daily work
sections.text: An editorial reading can examine devotion through repetition: planning a meal, learning restrictions and sustaining daily observance. It should also make room for participants’ own motives and the labour of cooks and carers. Historical restrictions surrounding widowhood deserve study without treating them as desirable rules or speaking for present-day women. The useful next step is an attributed account of how one household or community kitchen adapts its food, rather than a universal recipe.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Kartika is a cultural browsing cue; the calendar has no confirmed current-year date. Habisha Dalma is a food to ask about, but a named venue must confirm its menu and serving day before it becomes a recommendation. No household invitation, public meal, host consent or temple access has been established by this research.

pages.name: Magha Brata
pages.traditional_month: Magha
pages.observance_type: month-long brata; related Magha Saptami pilgrimage
pages.lead: Magha Brata places devotion within the daily rhythm of a month. At Chandrabhaga, a particular morning of that month also brings a pilgrimage gathering. Reading the two together reveals connections between household discipline, sacred stories and place, while keeping their food practices distinct.

sections.title: The month and the pilgrimage day
sections.text: Mahanti describes Magha Brata as a month-long observance, particularly among widows, beginning the day after Pausa purnima. His account includes a visit to Chandrabhaga on Magha Saptami. Dash lists the vow without further detail. These descriptions do not establish that every observer travels to Konark.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 26,52 / PDF42,68; Dash printed16 / PDF2

sections.title: Samba, the Sun and a sacred landscape
sections.text: In the legend recounted by Mahanti, Samba, Krishna’s son, suffers an illness after his father’s curse and recovers through bathing and worship of Surya. This is a devotional explanation for the place’s importance. It is not evidence of a cure or a dated biography.
sections.locator: Printed52 / PDF68

sections.title: A dated historical reference
sections.text: Bishan Swarup’s Konarka: The Black Pagoda of Orissa was published by the Government of Bengal in 1910. On printed 42, while discussing the Prachi Mahatmyam, he mentions the fair on Magha’s bright seventh day. The inspected title page establishes the book’s year. This is a dated reference to the pilgrimage tradition, not a founding date for Magha Brata or proof of uninterrupted annual practice.
sections.locator: Title PDF4; printed 42 / PDF49; preface PDF6 dated 23 September 1910

sections.title: What the food evidence actually says
sections.text: Mahanti describes fasting with one meal daily, preferably havishanna. He gives neither its ingredients nor a cooking method in the Magha entry. The name is recorded as a vow meal; a Kartika Habisha Dalma recipe cannot simply be transferred to it. Local accounts are needed to explain what people prepare, share and avoid.
sections.locator: Printed52 / PDF68

sections.title: Related observances remain distinct
sections.text: Rath and colleagues place Magha Saptami on Magha’s bright seventh day and Samba Dashami on Pausa’s bright tenth. Their 2015 article describes sunrise prayers and the Chandrabhaga fair. Odisha Tourism also associates the beach with Magha Saptami. Shared solar devotion does not make these observances one calendar event or give them a common menu.
sections.locator: Rath et al printed 94 / PDF3, Rituals and Festivals; Tourism introductory paragraph

sections.title: What remains unknown about history
sections.text: The 2015 article points to Sarala’s Mahabharata as a literary witness to pilgrimage. The exact passage and edition have not been recovered here. No complete identified Odia Magha Brata katha, earliest local observance date or independently documented household recipe has been established. The 1910 book’s reference to a sacred text cannot supply those missing dates.
sections.locator: Rath et al printed 93 / PDF2; Swarup printed 42 / PDF49

sections.title: Significance and the work of observance
sections.text: An editorial reading can follow how the commitment of a month is sustained through ordinary work: obtaining food, preparing one meal and arranging daily worship. A fair involves another setting, with travel, shared spaces and potentially different participants. Future interviews should ask which practices belong to the household vow and which belong to the pilgrimage, allowing participants to describe their own reasons and variations.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Magha supplies a cultural season to explore. No current-year pilgrimage date, special menu, serving place, host consent or access arrangement has been verified. The tourism events page could not be fetched, so its indexed date range is not used for planning. The Chandrabhaga destination page supports a cultural association, not a booking or meal promise.

pages.name: Baisakha Brata
pages.traditional_month: Baisakha, described as a lunar month by Mahanti
pages.lead: Baisakha Brata joins a month of devotion to a repeated evening meal. The food matters through its place in a daily sequence of worship, reading and restraint. Broader Vaishakha stories also give food another role: hospitality to people travelling in the heat.

sections.title: A month of Vishnu devotion
sections.text: Mahanti describes Baisakha Brata throughout the lunar month, observed by married women and widows. Worship of Vishnu or a temple visit, together with reading the Vishnu Purana, precedes the meal. He says no formal brata is worn. Dash also lists Baisakha, but supplies no further description. These accounts do not establish a universal household rule or current participation rate.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed 45 / PDF61; Dash printed 16 / PDF2

sections.title: The meal: havishanna or kechudi
sections.text: Mahanti names havishanna or kechudi as the single meal taken towards evening. He supplies no proportions, grain or pulse variety, vegetables, seasoning or cooking method. The two names are retained without turning them into a fixed recipe or assuming they denote exactly the same preparation. A local account should explain how the meal is made and who shares it.
sections.locator: Printed 45 / PDF61

sections.title: A comparative story of hospitality
sections.text: In V. D. N. Rao’s condensed Skanda Purana telling, King Kirtiman encounters Vasishtha’s disciples offering shade, fruit and drinks to travellers. After learning about Vaishakha, he extends such service across his kingdom. Vishnu protects his devotion when Yama objects to its extraordinary results. This is a religious narrative from a broader tradition, not a documented Odisha king or an identified local Baisakha katha.
sections.locator: Web chapter 28, King Kirtiman paragraphs

sections.title: Food given and food eaten
sections.text: Rao’s account commends supplying water, meals and shelter in Vaishakha. These gifts belong to its account of charity. They do not establish the ingredients of an Odisha observer’s evening meal. Mahanti’s reference to reading the Vishnu Purana likewise does not identify this Skanda Purana story as the text read locally.
sections.locator: Rao web chapter 28, water-charity paragraphs; Mahanti printed 45 / PDF61

sections.title: History still needs its own evidence
sections.text: No dated origin for the Odisha vow or complete identified Odia telling has been established here. Search-index results point to museum catalogue entries titled Baisakha Mahatmya, but the catalogue originals could not be retrieved in this run. A title match cannot identify the work recited by a household, date the custom or prove separate textual variants. Manuscript contents remain unread.

sections.title: Significance and the questions food opens
sections.text: An editorial interpretation can follow two kinds of work: sustaining one’s own observance and offering refreshment to others. The comparison invites questions about kitchens, ingredients, water provision and learning across generations. It does not prove that a particular Odisha practice descended from the comparative story. Pana Sankranti, Akshaya Tritiya and the month-long vow require their own evidence; sharing a seasonal setting is not enough to merge their foods or histories.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Baisakha is a cultural browsing cue, not a verified annual appointment. A solar month label, a lunar observance and a specific festival day should be checked against the relevant local calendar before travel. No current-year dates, serving venue, household invitation, host consent or special menu have been verified.

kechudi — named evening meal alternative; preparation unspecified

pages.name: Guru Panchami
pages.traditional_month: Conflicted: Bhadrava in Mahanti; Ashwina in Dash; Phalguna in Ojha’s Brihaspati account
pages.observance_type: brata / teacher devotion; same-name identity unresolved
pages.lead: Guru Panchami opens a question about whom a community honours as its guru. The accounts found here point to teachers, the seven sages and Brihaspati, the divine teacher. They cannot yet be joined into one calendar, story or menu.

sections.title: Teachers and disciples in one Odisha account
sections.text: Mahanti places the vow on Bhadrava’s bright fifth day, after Ganesh Chaturthi. He associates it with disciples honouring teachers in residential gurukulas. His next paragraph describes married women fasting and honouring the seven sages in relation to menstrual purity beliefs. These are the author’s descriptions; the beliefs are not adopted as judgments about women or their bodies.
sections.locator: Printed47–48 / PDF63–64

sections.title: Three calendar statements, identities still open
sections.text: Dash’s 2006 inventory assigns Guru Panchami to Ashwina and separately names Roosi Panchami. Mahanti gives Bhadrava. In her February2022 essay, Tulasi Ojha assigns a Guru Panchami dedicated to Brihaspati to Phalguna’s bright fifth day, and treats Rishi Panchami separately in Bhadrava. The discrepancy may involve different uses of the name, differing accounts or error. The evidence does not yet decide between these explanations.
sections.locator: Dash printed16 / PDF2; Mahanti printed47–48 / PDF63–64; Ojha printed107–109 / viewer109–111

sections.title: Brihaspati: an attributed devotional episode
sections.text: Ojha presents Brihaspati as adviser to the gods. She recalls his sending his son Kacha to Shukracharya to learn the Sanjivani mantra despite the danger. This is an episode in her account of the divine teacher, not a recovered Odisha household brata-katha or a historical event.
sections.locator: Guru Panchami Katha, printed107–108 / viewer109–110

sections.title: Food evidence: fasting, with the menu unknown
sections.text: Mahanti reports upabasha in the women’s observance, but names no dish, ingredients, offering, water rule, duration or fast-breaking meal for Guru Panchami. The panchamruta footnote on printed47 belongs to the earlier Ananta passage, not to this vow. Ojha’s milk, banana and other-fruit offerings occur in her separate Rishi Panchami temple account; they have not been assigned to Guru Panchami.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed47–48 / PDF63–64 and footnote34 context; Ojha printed109 / viewer111

sections.title: What can be said about history
sections.text: The sources establish published descriptions, not a founding date. Mahanti calls the practice extinct and links that to the disappearance of gurukulas, but supplies no statewide survey or dated institutional series in this passage. That statement is not sufficient to declare the observance absent today. A modern article using the name likewise does not establish living practice.

sections.title: Significance without flattening differences
sections.text: An editorial reading can explore gratitude towards teachers, the transmission of knowledge and the authority attached to ritual instruction. It should also ask whose work and restrictions sustain an observance. The comparison is most useful when participants can explain their own names, stories and food rules. A complete cultural history needs those situated accounts alongside identifiable editions.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: This entry is a reading lead. Its unresolved identity and month prevent a dependable seasonal recommendation. No current-year date, public ceremony, consenting host, serving venue or special menu is verified. A publication mentioning an observance does not establish an invitation to take part.

questions: Can a named local community distinguish Guru Panchami from Rushi/Rishi Panchami and Guru Purnima?
Which calendar rule and deity belong to each local use of the name?
Can an identified Odia brata-katha, imprint and food passages be recovered?
What dated evidence supports the gurukula association or claims of decline?
What offerings, fasting rules, fast-breaking food and preparation are described by willing local participants?
Can the 2022 essay’s print images and cited textual sources be collated?

pages.name: Rushi Panchami
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava / Bhadraba
pages.observance_type: brata / seven-sages observance with a Puri temple expression
pages.lead: Rushi Panchami brings gratitude to the sages into Odisha’s ritual year. Its Puri accounts connect listening to a sacred story with offerings at Markandeswar. That temple setting gives food a specific ritual role; household meals still need their own evidence.

sections.title: A place in the ritual calendar
sections.text: Mahimohan Tripathy’s July2003 temple-festival survey places Rishi Panchami on the fifth day of Bhadraba’s bright fortnight. The2021 Lakshmi essay lists Rishipanchami among her temple festivals. These dated publications support the traditional calendar and association, not a date or programme for a particular year.
sections.locator: Tripathy printed39 / PDF3; Mohanty and Mohanty printed22 / PDF2

sections.title: The seven sages and a short sacred story
sections.text: Tulasi Ojha’s2022 essay names Kashyapa, Atri, Bharadwaja, Vishwamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni and Vasishtha. She links their worship to respect for inherited sacred learning. Her brief story tells of a Brahmin couple reborn as a bull and a female dog, released through service to the seven sages. This is an attributed ritual narrative, not a historical event or a complete recovered brata-katha.
sections.locator: Printed108 / viewer110

sections.title: Mahalakshmi at Markandeswar
sections.text: Ojha describes Sridevi travelling from the Ratnasimhasana to Markandeswar tank. After ceremonial bathing, Varuna and the seven sages are invoked; she hears the Rishi Panchami story read by the Pujapanda and returns after arati.
sections.locator: Printed109 / viewer111

sections.title: A story pictured in the temple
sections.text: Acharya’s2013 article describes a painting inside the Jagamohan showing Lakshmi hearing the Rishipanchami vow from Markandeya. He also lists Rishipanchami among occasions linking Markandeswar’s rites with Jagannath temple. A depicted sage and a performing priest occupy different levels of this account: one belongs to the sacred scene, the other to the ritual description. The article does not date the painting.
sections.locator: Printed106–107 / PDF3–4

sections.title: Food as an offering
sections.text: Ojha names milk, banana and other fruit as naivedya. Her passage supplies neither a complete recipe nor a household fast-breaking menu. She also reports women observing the vow in relation to menstrual-purity beliefs; these are attributed beliefs, not judgments about women’s bodies. A temple offering cannot establish what every household eats.
sections.locator: Printed108–109 / viewer110–111

sections.title: What the published record can and cannot date
sections.text: The2003 calendar is the earliest dated publication inspected in this bounded pass that explicitly lists Rishi Panchami. It is not the earliest evidence in existence or a founding date. Dash’s2006 inventory separately names Roosi Panchami and Guru Panchami. The conflicting Guru accounts remain in their own profile; similarity in sages or calendar does not settle local equivalence. Older temple records and identifiable Odia katha editions are still needed.

sections.title: Why listening matters
sections.text: Read together, the descriptions invite a cultural question: how do a narrated story, a painted scene and a shared offering sustain respect for learning? This is an editorial interpretation. The next stage should ask willing participants how they understand the vow, who prepares the offerings, and how family practices differ. It should preserve disagreement instead of turning one temple account into a statewide rule.

sections.title: For the seasonal traveller
sections.text: Use the Bhadrava entry to explore the story and ask locally about the observance. No current-year date, public programme, access permission, consenting host or serving place is verified here. Milk and fruit are documented offerings in a published temple account, not an advertised menu. A full pana preparation, its distribution and household fasting dishes remain unverified.

pages.name: Gouri Brata
pages.traditional_month: Unresolved identity: Aswina Gouri Brata; Srabana Mangala Gauri is a comparison, not an adopted alias
pages.observance_type: brata / Gouri-related observances under identity research
pages.lead: Gouri Brata opens a path through women’s ritual art, storytelling and offerings. The published accounts do not yet describe one securely identified observance: an autumn drawing tradition, a Srabana Tuesday vow and a literary night vigil need to be understood in their own settings.

sections.title: A name in Odisha’s record
sections.text: Dash’s2006 inventory lists Gouri Brata without specifying its calendar or meal. Biswal and Dash’s2020 article places Gouri Brata and Durgastami Brata in Aswina and associates them with mandala-jhoti and wall images of Shiva and Durga. Its next sentences describe western Odisha Dusshera drawings. Those adjacent details should not all become a universal Gouri design.
sections.locator: Dash printed16 / PDF2; Biswal and Dash printed116–117 / PDF117–118, item8

sections.title: A night kept awake by stories
sections.text: In Sankarsan Malik’s2021 reading of Brajanath Badjena’s Chaturvinoda, Chanchalaksi observes Gouribrata as a night-long worship of Parvati. She asks Prince Mohananga to wait until the following day and proposes conversation through the night; he tells four stories. This is the scholar’s account of a literary framing scene, not a recovered household brata-katha or a witnessed ritual.
sections.locator: Printed/PDF412

sections.title: History: a literary lead, not a founding date
sections.text: Malik treats Chaturvinoda as an eighteenth-century work. His bibliography identifies S. N. Mishra’s edited Brajanath Granthabali, Orissa State Archives,1984. That edition was not recovered in this pass. The literary lead helps frame a historical investigation, but an inspected original passage, edition history and local evidence are needed before dating this form of Gouri Brata or claiming continuity to current practice.
sections.locator: Printed411–412 / PDF411–412; printed/PDF432, bibliography item20

sections.title: Mangala Gauri: a separate food comparison
sections.text: Mahanti describes Mangala Gauri, also called Srabani, on Srabana Tuesdays, beginning from the dark fortnight’s first tithi. Married and newly married women fast and worship Parvati’s image, wrapped in red cloth on a wooden pedestal. Fruit and pitha are offered as bhoga. He names no pitha varieties, recipe, quantities or fast-breaking meal. This food description remains attached to his named Srabani observance; it has not been assigned to the Aswina entry.
sections.locator: Printed46 / PDF62

sections.title: A Kashi narrative as a comparison
sections.text: In the Kashi-khanda account, the Sun installs Gabhastishvara and Mangala Gauri at Panchanada. His penance radiates unbearable heat; Shiva restores his awareness by touch. The Sun then praises the goddess in the Mangalashtaka. This is an attributed sacred narrative, not a dated history of Odisha’s Srabani vow.
sections.locator: Chapter49 verses26–44,55–69a

sections.title: Different calendar, different food roles
sections.text: The same text prescribes worship and a night vigil on Chaitra’s bright third day. Next morning, twelve unmarried girls receive sweet cooked food and a Brahmin couple is fed; the devotee then breaks the fast. Sesame and ghee are fire offerings, not a meal. These Kashi prescriptions remain separate from Mahanti’s Srabana-Tuesday fruit and pitha offerings. Neither account identifies a particular Odisha pitha recipe.
sections.locator: Kashi chapter49 verses80b–93; Mahanti printed46/PDF62

sections.title: What the comparison establishes
sections.text: A shared goddess name does not establish a shared household vow. The Kashi passage supplies a comparative narrative and prescription, but an original Odia text and named local practice are still needed to explain Srabani’s own story, transmission and meal. Its presence here deepens the existing research page without adding a duplicate observance or resolving the Aswina identity.

sections.title: A Gouri story from another context
sections.text: Under Gouri Panchami, Ojha retells Parvati’s response to Shiva calling her Kali: she undertakes austerities, and Brahma grants a golden complexion, making a blue lotus from the discarded dark colour. This is an attributed myth about the deity, not verified history or a judgment about skin colour. Ojha then discusses Jagulei worship. Mahanti separately describes Jagulai/Jagrata Gauri on Srabana’s dark fifth. These accounts do not establish that Gouri Panchami, Jagulai and Gouri Brata are interchangeable.
sections.locator: Ojha printed109 / viewer111; Mahanti printed75 / PDF91

sections.title: Food, drawing materials and the work of observance
sections.text: No named dish is yet securely established for the Aswina Gouri Brata entry. Rice used for ritual drawing cannot be counted as a meal, and the fruit/pitha comparison does not identify a particular pitha. Useful next questions concern who prepares the ritual space, who narrates the story, who fasts, and what is offered and subsequently eaten. These roles may differ between homes and observances.

sections.title: Significance to explore with participants
sections.text: The literary vigil and drawing account suggest ways to study devotion through time spent awake, stories exchanged and spaces prepared. This is an editorial reading, not evidence that the same practice links every source. Situated accounts from willing participants could explain how inherited knowledge is shared and whose labour sustains it.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: This is a reading page while the local identity is unresolved. No single season, annual date, special menu, public ceremony, serving venue or consenting host is established. A traveller should first identify the local name and practice before using a calendar or looking for food.

pages.name: Bipattarini Brata
pages.traditional_month: Odisha calendar unresolved; Bengali Ashar comparison only
pages.observance_type: brata / protective vow under regional identity research
pages.lead: Bipattarini Brata brings the hope of protection into a household’s ritual life. To understand its food culture in Odisha, the first task is to identify which story and practice a family follows. The name appears in an Odisha inventory; the fuller accounts recovered here come from Bengali settings and remain comparisons.

sections.title: What the Odisha record establishes
sections.text: Dash’s2006 inventory names Bipattarini Brata but supplies no dedicated story, date or menu. Mahanti describes a Tarini Brata on Ashadha’s bright fourth, with a fast, red thread and the Ghatagaon Tarini shrine as context. Similar names and protective themes do not establish that these are one observance. Tarini’s calendar is therefore not assigned to Bipattarini.
sections.locator: Dash printed16 / PDF2; Mahanti printed46 / PDF62

sections.title: A riverbank story of protection: Bengali comparison
sections.text: In Amrita Bhattacharyya’s2011 account of Bengali brata stories, Narada meets women worshipping Durga beside the Kartoya river. He recalls Shiva invoking Durga while drinking the poison from the churning of the ocean, and Yashoda tying a protective armlet on Krishna. Krishna also remembers Durga in danger. This is the article’s attributed sacred narrative, not verified events or an inspected Odia household text.
sections.locator: PDF16–17, Bipattarini paragraph

sections.title: Historical evidence and its limits
sections.text: The2011 article places this Bengali observance in Ashar. Its bibliography cites Rama Devi’s Meyeder Bratakatha, edited by Gopalchandra Bhattacharya, without a known year; that edition was not recovered. These modern records establish published descriptions, not the vow’s founding date, earliest textual witness or route of transmission into Odisha.
sections.locator: PDF16 and PDF19 note1

sections.title: Fruit, sweets and the number thirteen: Rajpur comparison
sections.text: Rajpur’s Bipattarini Chandibari in West Bengal describes vegetarian food on the preceding day, then fruit and sweets when breaking the fast. Thirteen kinds of fruit are offered: the temple explains twelve as the year’s months and one as the worshipper. It also describes a red thread with thirteen knots. No fruit varieties, sweet names, recipe or quantities are given. This is the temple’s own account, not an established Odisha menu.
sections.locator: About section: previous-day, fast-breaking, thirteen-fruit and thread paragraphs; address footer

sections.title: Keep the calendar attached to its place
sections.text: The Rajpur page’s general rule is a Tuesday between Rath Yatra and Ulto Rath in Bengali Ashar. Its dated banner calls21July2026 the fourth of Shravan1433. The different calendar labels have not been reconciled here; neither becomes an Odisha annual date. A dated temple announcement also does not verify present service or food availability.
sections.locator: About section annual festival paragraphs and announcement banner; research limitation appended

sections.title: How food can carry meaning
sections.text: The Rajpur account distinguishes food withheld, food offered and food eaten after a fast. That sequence offers a way to ask about household memory and care: who chooses the fruit, prepares food, tells the story and shares the meal? These are research questions for Odisha participants, rather than conclusions that the same rules apply everywhere. The number thirteen in this account does not establish a historical link with the saying Bara Masa, Tera Parba.

sections.title: What is still missing locally
sections.text: An identifiable Odia brata-katha or a situated account from Odisha is still needed. The queen-and-friend story found in a modern translated devotional page is another transmission lead, not a verified local version or independent proof of origin. No specific Odisha dish, cooking method, household variation, historical start date or human review is established.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Use this page to learn what to ask about, rather than as a food booking or festival-date guide. There is no verified Odisha serving venue, public meal, host invitation or current date attached to this entry. If a consenting local host shares a practice, record its name, place and distinction between offering and meal before recommending it to visitors.

pages.name: Sankata Chaturthi
pages.traditional_month: Magha account; relation to monthly Ganesh vow unresolved
pages.observance_type: brata / chaturthi observance under identity research
pages.lead: A rice cake shaped in the hand offers one way into Sankata Chaturthi’s food culture. The written accounts preserve both kitchen detail and uncertainty: the cake’s name and preparation vary, and descriptions of the observance do not all name the same deity or calendar rule.

sections.title: An Odisha account in Magha
sections.text: Pratap Kumar Dash’s April 2006 survey places Sankata Chaturthi in Magha and names Shiva and Parvati as the deities worshipped. This is a published description without a named household or locality. It establishes an account to investigate, rather than a uniform rule for Odisha.
sections.locator: Printed16 / PDF2

sections.title: Bundi in the paragraph, Bindi in the note
sections.text: The April article’s food paragraph prints Bundi; its note 17 prints Bindi. The note describes a handful-sized cake of powdered fried unboiled rice, molasses and coconut scraps. The spelling difference remains visible. This rice preparation cannot be silently replaced by a familiar sweet sold under a similar name, nor transferred to the separately listed Nagala Chaturthi.
sections.locator: Printed17 / PDF3 food paragraph and printed18 / PDF4 note17; editorial identity boundary appended

sections.title: A second kitchen description from the same author
sections.text: In December 2006, Dash calls the food Bindi, also known as hundi. He describes khali, a boiled dough of sundried rice powder, with molasses, coconut, black pepper, ajowan and cardamom; ghee helps form handful-sized cakes. This account associates the observance with Shiva. It gives no quantities or complete cooking sequence, and differs from April’s fried-rice wording. The two articles share an author and are not independent corroboration.
sections.locator: Printed48 / PDF48 byline; printed49 / PDF49 Sankata paragraph. Web-extracted text; page images unavailable.

sections.title: A recurring Ganesh vow in another account
sections.text: Mahanti describes Sankati Chaturthi and Binayak Chaturthi as recurring vows on the fourth lunar day of the dark and bright fortnights respectively. Women and men fast and worship Ganesh; the Sankati account waits for the Moon in the evening. A Tuesday occurrence is called Angarki, associated devotionally with relief from danger. The inspected passage names no food. Its relation to Dash’s Magha Shiva–Parvati account remains unresolved.
sections.locator: Printed43–44 / PDF59–60, Sankati and Binayak heading

sections.title: What the food can help us ask
sections.text: The handful-sized cake brings attention to preparation as an act of care: whose hands shape it, who teaches the method, and how is it shared? Those are questions for local accounts. The sources inspected here do not establish whether this particular cake is first offered, eaten to end a fast, or served as a household meal. Those roles should be recorded separately.

sections.title: History and the story still need an identifiable text
sections.text: The 2006 publications document descriptions; they do not date the beginning of this observance. No complete, identifiable Odia brata-katha was recovered in this pass. A historical book scan by B. A. Gupte was recovered as a wider comparison lead, but its relevant story pages have not been inspected. Neither similar names nor an older general book establish a line of transmission into Odisha.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Treat Magha as an attributed cultural lead, not a confirmed annual event date or guarantee that a shop will sell this food. There is no verified serving place, public meal or host invitation attached to this entry. Ask a willing local host which name, recipe and calendar their household follows before turning the association into a visitor recommendation.

pages.name: Radhastami Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava, bright fortnight, eighth lunar day
pages.lead: Radhastami brings the celebration of Radha’s appearance into songs, worship and the rhythm of fasting and eating. Its food culture is not yet a reliable list of special dishes: the evidence takes us through a meal inside a sacred story, offerings in a text, and prasada shared after a fast.

sections.title: The observance and its season
sections.text: Dash’s Odisha inventory identifies Radhastami with Radha worship. Mahanti places it on Bhadrava’s bright eighth lunar day and describes flower-decorated Radha–Krishna images, fasting and devotional song. Tripathy’s 2003 Jagannath festival list gives the same lunar-day rule. These are source descriptions, not evidence that every household follows an identical practice.
sections.locator: Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed48/PDF64; Tripathy printed39/PDF3

sections.title: An Odia story told through questions
sections.text: In Shubhapallaba’s verse text, Rukmini asks Krishna about Radha; Satyabhama asks how the eternal Radha relates to her earthly life. Radha accompanies Krishna’s descent and appears as a child on a lotus in Kalindi. Vrishabhanu brings her home to Queen Chanchala. When Narada assures her that Krishna has come to earth, she asks for food, and her mother hurries to her. This is an attributed sacred narrative, not a verified historical birth.
sections.locator: Opening dialogue; Krishna’s answer; lotus-child episode; Narada and Chanchala meal episode

sections.title: Another textual account
sections.text: The Padma Purana translation tells of Lilavati joining a Radhastami observance and later being rescued by Vishnu’s messengers. In its Radha appearance passage, Vrishabhanu finds her on sacrificial ground. This differs from the lotus setting in the Odia text. The accounts remain distinct; their relationship and transmission into particular Odisha households have not been established.
sections.locator: Padma Brahma-khanda chapter7, verses13–24 and25–42; Odia lotus-child episode

sections.title: Food inside the story is not a festival recipe
sections.text: The Odia episode describes Chanchala bringing food of six tastes, without naming dishes. Its ritual directions include fasting, flowers, akshata, shriphala and tambula. These are textual categories, not a recovered cooked menu. The story’s meal cannot be promoted to a household recipe or claim about current offerings.
sections.locator: Narada/meal episode; Brata Bidhana ending

sections.title: Offerings and the meal after fasting
sections.text: Mahanti describes devotees ending the fast towards midday with temple prasada, explained as cooked food offered to the deities. The passage names no dishes, quantities or kitchen. The Padma chapter describes fruit among the offerings, but supplies no fruit varieties or Odisha preparation. Prasada names a ritual relationship to food; it does not by itself identify a sweet, pitha or complete menu.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed48/PDF64; Padma Brahma-khanda7, verses13–20

sections.title: Puri and Sakhigopal need their own context
sections.text: Behera’s 2019 Puri account describes taking Sudarsan to four ashrams on Radhastami. It does not specify a household menu. Mahanti separately places Radha-pada darshana at Sakhigopal on Kartika’s Aonla Navami. That foot-viewing occasion should not be moved into a Bhadrava itinerary simply because both observances concern Radha. Current routes and visitor access remain unverified.
sections.locator: Behera printed103/PDF4; Mahanti printed48/PDF64

sections.title: What is known about textual history
sections.text: The Odia post is dated 25 August 2020 and carries differing verse signatures: Kshetramohan, Kshetra and Kshetrabasi. The printed exemplar and author identity remain unverified. Modern publication dates do not date the beginning of the vow. Manuscript-catalogue search leads were found, but the original catalogue could not be recovered for this pass; they remain unverified leads in the research record.

sections.title: A recent Konark announcement, kept in its scope
sections.text: Radha Govind Dham Konark advertised Radhashtami sankirtan for 19 September 2026, 9:30 AM–2:00 PM. On 9 October its page still labelled this upcoming. The announcement establishes an advertised programme at a named Odisha institution; it does not show that the programme occurred, identify a meal, or confirm current visitor access.
sections.locator: Home-page Upcoming Event banner and address footer, read9October2026

sections.title: Why the distinctions matter
sections.text: Read together, these accounts invite attention to several ways food enters devotion: a parent’s care in a story, something offered to a deity, and a meal received after abstaining. This is an editorial reading of the records, not a claim that one caused the others. A useful local account would explain who cooks, who offers, who shares and which names the household uses.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Use Bhadrava’s bright eighth as a cultural research window. Confirm the year’s local date and ask the host what, if anything, is open to visitors. No particular Radhastami dish, serving venue or invitation is verified here. General prasada descriptions and a past programme notice are not food-booking information.

pages.name: Shibaratri Brata
pages.traditional_month: Phalguna, dark fortnight; night associated with the fourteenth lunar day
pages.lead: A day without food leads into a night of wakefulness. Shibaratri’s cultural story connects hunger, leaves, lamps and the hope that worship can change a life. To understand its food culture, we need to ask what is withheld, what is offered and what is eaten afterwards.

sections.title: Names and season
sections.text: Dash lists Shibaratri Brata in Phalguna as Shiva worship. Mahanti discusses Maha Shivaratri as Jagara, spanning the dark-fortnight thirteenth/fourteenth night. His recurring Shiva Pradosha entry is separate. These descriptions do not establish an annual date or one rule for every household.
sections.locator: Dash printed 16/PDF 2; Mahanti printed 44/PDF 60 and 103–105/PDF 119–121

sections.title: A vigil, then a meal
sections.text: Mahanti describes daylong fasting and night vigil, with devotees breaking the fast after the Mahadipa is lit atop the temple. A particular temple’s annual timing still needs confirmation.
sections.locator: Printed 105–106/PDF 121–122

sections.title: The hunter in Mahanti’s telling
sections.text: Mahanti tells of Chitrabhanu’s previous life as a hunter. Stranded at night, he takes shelter in a bilva tree, dropping leaves onto an unseen linga below. Hunger keeps him awake. The unwitting worship brings him to Shiva’s abode and eventual rebirth as a king. This is a sacred story, not a dated historical event.
sections.locator: Printed 106/PDF 122

sections.title: Gurudruha and the deer
sections.text: The Shiva Purana translation’s chapter 40 begins with Gurudruha seeking food for his hungry family. From a bilva tree he watches a watering place; his movements drop water and leaves onto a linga. The deer ask leave to care for their young and promise to return. Their return changes him: he lowers his weapon and releases them. Shiva appears and names him Guha. This account differs from Mahanti’s Chitrabhanu ending; no textual genealogy between them has been demonstrated.
sections.locator: Kotirudra-samhita 40, verses 4–20, 27–39, 49–85 and 89–95

sections.title: Gaja pitha: a name with an unfinished recipe
sections.text: Mahanti names gaja pitha as a Shiva offering, but gives no recipe here. The name does not identify it with chhena gaja, Puri Gaja or the separately documented Bada Osha preparation.
sections.locator: Printed 105/PDF 121; comparison boundary explained in the linked Gaja dossier

sections.title: Ingredients used in worship
sections.text: Mahanti describes milk, yoghurt, ghee, honey, bilva leaves and water in the linga’s bathing sequence. Ritual bathing materials are not a verified fast-breaking menu.
sections.locator: Printed 105/PDF 121

sections.title: An Odia poem looks inward
sections.text: The Wikisource text of Gopabandhu Das’s Shibaratri, in Abakash Chinta, begins with fasting, a lamp and a planned night vigil. Its speaker then asks whether outward light can dispel inward darkness. The ending turns wakefulness into an appeal for awareness and worthy action throughout life. This is a reading of the attributed poem, not evidence that households recite it as their brata katha. The scanned edition and composition date remain to be checked.
sections.locator: Opening couplet, inward questioning and concluding verses; chapter oldid=58885 and collection attribution

sections.title: One divine story can belong to different occasions
sections.text: Mahanti separately describes Sitala Sasthi in Jyestha as Shiva–Parvati’s marriage observance in Puri sasana villages and Sambalpur. A marriage explanation alone cannot identify a festival’s local date.
sections.locator: Printed 105/PDF 121

sections.title: History and local practice still to recover
sections.text: The inspected sources establish named accounts and literary reflections, not the earliest Odisha observance. Two Odia book listings were discovered, but their detail pages failed to load; neither edition nor contents is verified. Original Odia katha, manuscript dates, local preparation and household variation remain open. Government tourism and endowment pages also failed direct retrieval; their indexed descriptions have not been promoted into current schedules or food offers.

sections.title: Reading the food culture
sections.text: Hunger drives the hunter narratives; abstaining from food shapes the vigil; an offering receives a particular name. These connections make food central even when a full menu is missing. They suggest questions about care, restraint and sharing, rather than permission to invent a standard festival plate. This is an editorial interpretation of the saved accounts.

sections.title: For a seasonal visitor
sections.text: Treat Phalguna as a research window and confirm the local year’s date and permitted participation. Ask specifically about the locally named gaja pitha, its maker, ingredients and whether it is offered or served to visitors. No venue, invitation, portion, price or current food availability is verified here.

pages.name: Shri Krishna Janmastami Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrava, dark fortnight, eighth lunar day
pages.lead: Janmastami gathers attention around a child’s arrival at night. Fasting gives way to celebration, and food becomes part of welcoming and sharing. Its Odisha story moves between the household shrine and Jagannath’s ritual calendar, with differences that deserve to be remembered.

sections.title: A brata in the Odisha calendar
sections.text: Dash lists Shri Krishna Janmastami Brata in Bhadrab. Mahanti places it on Bhadrava’s dark eighth and describes observance in some Odisha homes and temples, with fasting and wakefulness until midnight. He notes that no formal brata is worn.
sections.locator: Dash printed 16/PDF 2; Mahanti printed 47/PDF 63

sections.title: The birth story: fear, protection and an exchange
sections.text: In the Bhagavata translation, Krishna appears to Devaki and Vasudeva with divine attributes. Afraid of Kamsa, Devaki asks him to conceal that form. He becomes an infant; the guards sleep and the locked doors open. Vasudeva crosses the Yamuna and places Krishna beside the sleeping Yasoda, returning with her daughter. This is an attributed sacred narrative, not a verified birth chronology.
sections.locator: 10.3 chapter summary and verses 7–10, 28–30, 46–51

sections.title: When does the fast end?
sections.text: The Odisha government overview says devotees break the fast after the symbolic midnight birth. Mahanti describes breaking it with the following day’s Nandotsava. These broad accounts do not establish one clock time or rule for every household; a named local practice must be checked before giving instructions.
sections.locator: Government Janmastami subsection; Mahanti printed 47, 82/PDF 63, 98

sections.title: The cradle and the shared offering
sections.text: Mahanti’s general puja description has the infant image rocked in a cradle after midnight amid devotional singing. For Nandotsava he describes foods prepared at homes and temples, offered to Krishna and then taken as prasada. He names no dishes in this passage.
sections.locator: Printed 81–82/PDF 97–98; general puja description distinguished from Odisha-specific brata entry

sections.title: Milk foods in the sacred narrative
sections.text: Bhagavata 10.5.14 describes cowherds celebrating by splashing and smearing dairy substances. The inspected English translation names curd, condensed milk, butter and water. This is festive play within the story; it does not establish a household recipe or an Odisha fast-breaking plate.
sections.locator: 10.5.14 translation; English terms retained with translation-specific scope

sections.title: Puri: a sequence of occasions
sections.text: Mahimohan Tripathy’s 2003 temple account places Krishna Janma on Bhadraba’s dark eighth, Nandotsav the next day, and a series of Krishna-lila observances afterwards, including Banabhoji and Kolibika. The calendar connects the birth to enacted childhood episodes; it does not make their offerings interchangeable with Janmastami food.
sections.locator: Printed 39/PDF 3, Krishna Janma & Lila

sections.title: Food leads that still need the original evidence
sections.text: Search results identified accounts of Jeuta or Jeuda Bhoga before the birth ritual and a 2013 Odisha Review article on Banabhoji’s picnic dress. The institutional article and original PDF could not be retrieved in this run. Their indexed ingredient and food details remain research leads, not adopted recipes or visitor recommendations.

sections.title: A local calendar entry, with a limited claim
sections.text: ISKCON Bhubaneswar’s website lists Janmastami on 4 September 2026. This establishes the institution’s announced date only. It does not verify the event took place or that a particular dish was available.
sections.locator: Homepage events calendar, Janmastami entry; read 9 October 2026

sections.title: What the food culture helps us see
sections.text: Read together, the accounts make food part of waiting, welcoming and sharing. A fast can give the moment of birth a bodily rhythm; an offering becomes something received after worship. Dairy’s presence in the cowherd story adds another layer of meaning. This is an editorial reading of the sources, not a claim that all families explain their practice in these terms.

sections.title: History and regional differences remain open
sections.text: These sources document descriptions and sacred narratives, not the earliest Odisha observance. An original Odia Janmastami brata text, dated local witnesses and named household food accounts still need study. Mahanti places his dahi-handi description in Maharashtra and north India; that passage cannot supply an Odisha event or menu.

sections.text: Use Bhadrava as a research window, then confirm the local year’s date, the particular occasion and permission to participate. Ask whether food belongs to the midnight worship, Nandotsava or a later Krishna-lila rite. A cultural association does not establish a public meal. pages.name: Pusa Rabibara Brata
pages.traditional_month: Pausa; Sundays in the inspected Odia text
pages.lead: A wedding procession is still on the road and daylight is slipping away. In the Pusha Rabibara story, a bride asks the sun to wait. The request begins a tale that brings a royal household to the tulsi courtyard, where flowers, food and a Sunday vow become part of making amends.

sections.title: A seasonal Sunday vow
sections.text: Dash lists Pusa Rabibara Brata in Pausa as worship of the sun. The Odia text’s directions specify Sundays in Pusha. Dash separately lists Rabinarayan in Margasira; a shared solar dedication does not make these entries interchangeable.
sections.locator: Dash printed16/PDF2; scan PDF7, directions beginning after the account of the curse

sections.title: The prince and the merchant’s daughter
sections.text: The scanned katha opens with a king, queen and their son, who wants to marry after his companions have done so. A Brahmin intermediary finds a merchant’s daughter in Karnataka, and a wedding is arranged. These places and characters belong to the story; the text supplies no verified historical itinerary.
sections.locator: PDF2–5, opening royal household through marriage and return procession

sections.title: The sun is asked to pause
sections.text: On the return journey, the bride fears darkness will fall before the gifts and procession reach home. She asks Aditya to pause until they enter the palace. He grants the request. His mother, waiting for him, angrily curses whoever delayed his journey. When she learns why he is late, she tells him that the bride can seek relief through the Pusha Sunday vow.
sections.locator: PDF5–7, request to Aditya, delayed return and the mother’s response

sections.title: The story reaches the courtyard
sections.text: The bride becomes afflicted; the royal household seeks guidance from its religious advisers. She undertakes the vow and, in the story’s ending, recovers and prospers. The narrative presents devotion as the remedy. It is a sacred healing story, not medical evidence or advice to replace treatment.
sections.locator: PDF7–8, affliction, advice and concluding observance

sections.title: Preparing a place before sunrise
sections.text: The directions call for rising before sunrise on Pusha Sundays, bathing, preparing the area at the tulsi plant with cow dung, establishing a sun mandala, decorating with flowers and inviting a Brahmin for worship. These are directions in this textual witness; present-day household adaptations have not been documented here.
sections.locator: PDF7, ritual directions

sections.title: What the text offers
sections.text: The clearly legible offering terms on PDF7 include sugar, pitha, ripe fruit, bananas and coconut. The passage gives no named pitha variety, quantities or cooking method. Its list describes offerings for worship, not a verified fasting diet or public meal.
sections.locator: PDF7, offering lines after the instruction to invite a Brahmin; selected terms only, not full transcription

sections.title: A food name carried into the market
sections.text: In her essay Muan, Dr Jayashree Nanda reports that seasonal sweets are sold under names including Pusha Rabibara muan, Dhanu muan and Makara muan. This is an attributed cultural account. The shared naming context does not prove identical ingredients, and the essay does not identify a current seller for this observance.
sections.locator: Opening market-name paragraph, after visible author credit

sections.title: A wider Sunday practice, kept separate
sections.text: Mahanti’s weekly Rabibara entry describes sun worship, fasting with one meal towards evening and almsgiving. It does not explicitly identify those rules as Pusa Rabibara Brata. The Pausa profile therefore leaves the actual fast-breaking time and meal open.
sections.locator: Printed63/PDF79, separate weekly Rabibara entry

sections.title: History: a recovered text, an unresolved date
sections.text: Project Pothi’s scan gives us a readable textual witness. The Commons page credits Prateek Pattanaik with providing and scanning it, calls the author unknown and labels it part of Bratabali. Its eighteenth-century description and 8 February 1917 publication field have not been confirmed from an original imprint. They cannot establish when this vow began in Odisha.
sections.locator: Commons Summary and file history; PDF1–8 inspected without a verified original imprint

sections.title: How to read its significance
sections.text: The story places a bride’s journey within the sun’s daily movement, then brings the consequences into household worship. Food is part of the act of devotion, alongside a prepared courtyard, flowers and spoken guidance. The seasonal market name adds a different kind of memory: how an observance may help people name a sweet. This is an editorial interpretation, not a universal account of belief.
