sections.text: Ask about Pusha Rabibara muan during the locally observed Pausa season, and ask the maker what that name means in their practice. Confirm ingredients, preparation and current availability before planning a visit. Household worship requires an invitation; the textual offering list is not a restaurant menu. No seller, annual date or public serving arrangement is verified here.

pages.name: Binayaka Brata
pages.traditional_month: Bhadrab/Bhadrava; annual bright-fortnight fourth, distinguished from recurring Chaturthi vows
pages.lead: Twenty-one sweets become a small map of giving: one for Ganesha, ten for a Brahmin and ten for the person observing the vow. A recovered Binayaka booklet makes this division explicit. It offers a way to explore devotion through food, while a separate government record takes the printed history of a same-titled work back to 1936.

sections.title: The annual vow and its neighbours
sections.text: Dash lists Binayaka Brata in Bhadrab as Ganesh worship. Mahanti places annual Ganesh Puja on Bhadrava’s bright fourth and distinguishes it from recurring bright-fortnight Binayak and dark-fortnight Sankati vows. Their similar names do not establish identical menus or fasting rules.
sections.locator: Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed43–44/PDF59–60 and79/PDF95

sections.title: A booklet with more than one calendar passage
sections.text: The recovered booklet opens with Bhadraba bright-fortnight Chaturthi and a rule involving midday. Its later katha also names other months, including Srabana and Margasira. These passages need fuller textual comparison before their calendar relationships can be explained. No annual Gregorian date is calculated here.
sections.locator: PDF3/printed1 opening directions; PDF7–8/printed5–6 Sanskrit verses and Odia explanation

sections.title: Yudhishthira asks how to recover what was lost
sections.text: The katha frames its teaching through Suta’s narration to sages. Yudhishthira asks Krishna which deity he should worship to overcome his troubles and regain his kingdom. Krishna directs him to Ganapati and explains the vow. The text draws on a wider sacred world of exemplary devotees, then says Yudhishthira followed the teaching and recovered his kingdom. This is a devotional account of the vow’s power, not evidence that these events occurred historically or that the practice began in Odisha at that time.
sections.locator: PDF6–8/printed4–6 opening dialogue; PDF11–14/printed9–12 examples and conclusion

sections.title: A birth story is a different narrative layer
sections.text: Mahanti recounts another story: Parvati gives life to a boy made from sandalwood paste and asks him to guard her bath. A confrontation with Shiva leads to his beheading; he is revived with an elephant’s head. This attributed birth story explains Ganesha’s form. It is kept separate from the booklet’s dialogue about performing the vow.
sections.locator: Printed80–81/PDF96–97; short synopsis of this author’s version

sections.title: Twenty-one modaka and their distribution
sections.text: The booklet instructs the observer to prepare 21 modaka: ten go to a Brahmin, ten are eaten by the observer and one is offered to the deity. The later Odia directions describe the sweets as cooked with ghee. Flowers and fruit also appear in groups of 21. This is a prescription in one printed witness; it does not establish a universal household practice.
sections.locator: PDF6/printed4 directions; PDF9–10/printed7–8 Odia explanation, continuing over the page

sections.title: The recipe is still missing
sections.text: The inspected directions name modaka and ghee but do not give a complete ingredient list, measurements, shape or cooking sequence. A familiar modern modak recipe cannot simply fill these gaps. Neither the booklet’s name nor its allocation of sweets proves that every Odisha household makes the same preparation.

sections.title: From a household vow to a shared school meal
sections.text: Mahanti describes students decorating clay images, fasting before midday worship and breaking coconuts. Teachers and students later share an evening feast after arati. He also describes household pujas and women observing Vinayaka Brata. The feast’s dishes are unnamed; it cannot be treated as the booklet’s modaka distribution or a verified public meal today.
sections.locator: Printed79–80/PDF95–96; school and household settings

sections.title: What a 1937 record tells us
sections.text: A government catalogue published on 29 October 1937 lists Binayaka Brata Katha as an 8-page work published by Gobind Sahu of Ganjam in 1936. Entry 172 describes Sanskrit worship directions and an Odia vow story. It identifies Pharmacy Press, Berhampur, names Keshab Narayan Patnaik and records 1,000 copies. This documents a printed witness by 1936; it does not date the tradition’s beginning or measure readership.
sections.locator: Printed17/PDF17, entry 172; catalogue covers registrations in the quarter ending 31 March 1937

sections.title: Two book identities, not one dated scan
sections.text: The Gazette entry and the recovered Dharmagrantha Store booklet have not been matched as editions. The scan has two cover images, 12 printed text pages and an advertisement; no publication year or named author has been verified. Its cover says new impression. The 1936 date belongs to the separately catalogued work and must not be assigned to this scan.
sections.locator: Scan PDF1–2 cover, PDF14/printed12 ending and PDF15 advertisement; Gazette printed17/PDF17 entry 172

sections.title: Reading the significance through food
sections.text: The division of sweets makes food both an offering and a relationship between deity, ritual specialist and observer. The school feast presents a different setting of shared eating. Together they suggest questions about how devotion moves between household and institution, without assuming that one setting grew historically from the other. This is an editorial reading of the evidence.

sections.title: For the seasonal food guide
sections.text: Use Bhadrava Ganesh Chaturthi as a cultural browsing lead. Ask a willing maker what their household calls modaka, how it is prepared and how it is shared. Confirm the local date and any public food offer separately. School and household observances do not by themselves establish visitor admission. No serving venue or current availability is verified.

pages.name: Skanda Sasthi Brata
pages.traditional_month: Chaitra in Dash; Chaitra dark sixth in Mahanti, awaiting local almanac verification
pages.observance_type: brata / Kartikeya observance; Odisha practice unresolved
pages.lead: A festival name can survive in a calendar even when its place in everyday life is uncertain. Skanda Sasthi appears in an Odisha inventory, yet another writer says it is listed in almanacs without being observed in the state. Following that discrepancy reveals why the history of a deity, a vow and a seasonal meal must each be investigated.

sections.title: A name in the inventory, a question about practice
sections.text: Pratap Kumar Dash lists Skanda Sasthi Brata in Chaitra. J. C. Mahanti gives Chaitra’s dark-fortnight sixth, associates it with Kartikeya and says many panjis mention it, but that it is not observed in Odisha. His broad statement is an author’s account, not a present-day statewide survey. The two sources leave actual local practice unresolved.
sections.locator: Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed53/PDF69

sections.title: The deity has an Odisha history; the vow still needs one
sections.text: Kalyan Kumar Panda discusses a two-armed Karttikeya Mahasena image at the Kosalesvara temple, Baidyanath, riding a peacock and holding a vel. Panda favours a sixth-century date, while explicitly noting Vidya Dehejia’s disagreement with Charles Fabri’s dating. This is attributed art-historical context with a dating dispute. It cannot establish when Skanda Sasthi Brata began in Odisha.
sections.locator: Printed37–38/PDF1–2; cited archaeological studies not independently inspected

sections.title: A 1921 comparison from South India
sections.text: P. V. Jagadisa Ayyar’s South Indian Festivities was published in Madras in 1921. Its Skanda Sashti chapter places the festival on the bright-fortnight sixth in Arpisi, approximately October–November, and relates it to Subrahmanyam’s victory over Surapadma. That seasonal setting differs from the Chaitra entry in the Odisha accounts. It is retained as regional comparison, not used to replace their calendar.
sections.locator: Title page PDF6; chapter XXIII printed146/PDF151

sections.title: Six sparks and a divine child: Ayyar’s version
sections.text: In Ayyar’s telling, the gods ask Shiva for relief from Surapadma. Shiva emits six sparks; Agni and Vayu temper their intensity and carry them towards the Ganges. The sparks gather among reeds and become a radiant child with six faces and twelve hands. The Krithika nurses are then linked to the name Kartikeya. This is a synopsis of a sacred narrative in a South Indian book, not a recovered Odia brata-katha or historical event.
sections.locator: Printed147–148/PDF152–153; selected birth narrative within the chapter

sections.title: What the comparison says about offerings
sections.text: A footnote explains kavadi as a shoulder-borne pole whose ends carry pots containing milk or sugar according to the vow. The surrounding passage concerns devotion to Subrahmanyam and the Idumban story. It is not an Odisha food description, a complete Skanda Sasthi menu or a recipe. These items are therefore excluded from the Odisha seasonal-food association.
sections.locator: Printed148/PDF153 footnote2 and surrounding passage; Idumban account continues printed149/PDF154

sections.title: Where the Odisha food record is still blank
sections.text: Neither inspected Odisha calendar entry names an offering, fasting food or fast-breaking dish for this vow. No Odia katha or named household account was recovered in this batch. A generic list of fruit offerings, a South Indian temple food, or a dish from another Sasthi cannot fill that gap. The local food association remains unestablished.

sections.title: Do not merge Skanda Sasthi with Sathi Osha
sections.text: The existing Sathi Osha record concerns goddess Shashthi and Bhadraba’s bright sixth, with a separately sourced household food account. The shared sixth-day language is a reason to compare identities carefully, not evidence that the two observances share their deity, season, story or menu.

sections.title: Why this uncertainty belongs in the cultural story
sections.text: This entry offers a way to ask how printed calendars, deity worship and household observance relate. It would be premature to call Skanda Sasthi either a widespread living Odisha tradition or an extinct one. The next useful evidence is a dated local panji entry paired with a willing practitioner’s account, followed by inspection of any text they identify.

sections.title: For the seasonal food guide
sections.text: This is a research lead, not a recommendation to travel for a meal. Confirm the observance’s local identity and annual date before asking about its food. No Odisha dish, serving place, current availability, visitor access or host consent has been verified.

pages.name: Guru Purnima Brata
pages.traditional_month: Ashadha full moon in Mahanti and Bhubaneswar Math; Dash separately prints Pausa, unresolved
pages.observance_type: guru-honouring full-moon observance / brata identity under comparison
pages.lead: At two Rourkela-area gatherings in July 2024, reverence for a guru took different forms: students sought their teachers’ blessings at one, while children honoured their parents at the other. Prasad followed both programmes. These situated accounts give Guru Purnima a place in Odisha’s lived culture, while leaving open the history and menu of the household brata named in an older inventory.

sections.title: Ashadha and Pausa: retain the disagreement
sections.text: Dash’s 2006 inventory prints Guru Purnima Brata in Pausa. Mahanti identifies Ashadha’s full moon as Vyasa or Guru Purnima, and Bhubaneswar Math’s 2026–2027 list likewise uses Ashadha Purnima. The institution’s calendar supports its own observance; it does not decide whether Dash’s Pausa entry is an error or a different local identity. Guru Panchami remains a separate research entry.
sections.locator: Dash printed16/PDF2; Mahanti printed22/PDF38; Math calendar PDF2 row6

sections.title: Why Vyasa is honoured
sections.text: Mahanti attributes this full moon to the birth of Vyasa, son of Parasara and Satyabati, traditionally revered for arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahabharata. In this account, remembering Vyasa becomes an occasion to honour spiritual teachers and the relationships through which learning is passed on. This is a religious explanation of significance, not an independently dated biography or proof of the festival’s beginning.
sections.locator: Printed22/PDF38; the religious chronology footnote is not adopted as historical dating

sections.title: A historical comparison: monastic Vyasa Puja in 1921
sections.text: In South Indian Festivities, published in Madras in 1921, P. V. Jagadisa Ayyar describes Vyasa Puja on Ashadha’s full moon, especially among renunciants. His explanation links veneration of Vyasa with Adi Shankara and concern for the welfare of the wider world. The publication documents this interpretation by 1921; it does not establish the ceremony’s origin or an Odisha household lineage.
sections.locator: Printed85/PDF94; title page PDF6. Only opening two pages of chapter XIV inspected for this profile

sections.title: Rice and limes in the South Indian comparison
sections.text: Ayyar describes rice laid on new cloth with lime fruits placed above it for invoking Shankara and his four disciples. After worship, the rice is distributed to be taken home and mixed with household stocks. His next page interprets rice and new cloth through Lakshmi and limes through wishes for success. These are his ritual description and symbolic reading. They are neither a cooked meal recipe nor verified Odisha practice.
sections.locator: Printed85–86/PDF94–95; regional comparison, not an Odisha food association

sections.title: A Bhubaneswar memory with an uncertain festival date
sections.text: The Math’s institutional history quotes Swami Brahmeswarananda remembering an ordination during a 1924 stay by Mahapurush Maharaj. He qualifies the occasion as probably Guru Purnima. That uncertainty must remain: the reminiscence is a lead for local monastic history, not a securely dated festival witness. The large prasad distribution described immediately before it belongs to a separate 1923 Vasanti Puja account and is not assigned to Guru Purnima.
sections.locator: Printed45/PDF25; title and author printed21/PDF1; original memoir not independently inspected

sections.title: Teachers, parents and prasad in Rourkela
sections.text: Vivekananda Kendra reports celebrations on 21 July 2024 at Vedvyas Sanskrit College and the GRP Training School in Rourkela. At the college, students sought teachers’ blessings after ritual worship. At the school programme, children washed their parents’ feet and sought blessings. The organiser records prasad distribution at both gatherings. These are specific reported events, not proof that every Odisha family follows the same form.
sections.locator: Dated post; Vedvyas and Rourkela programme paragraphs

sections.title: Cooked prasad: a dated plan, not a confirmed meal
sections.text: Bhubaneswar Math’s 2026–2027 calendar lists Guru Purnima on 29 July 2026 and marks it C.P., explained as cooked prasad to be distributed. This provides a named institutional food plan. The inspected calendar does not identify dishes, document completed distribution or confirm a serving offer now. Its date is kept in the evidence record rather than presented as a recurring date for all Odisha observances.
sections.locator: PDF2 row6 and C.P. legend; Odia PDF1 row6 and anna-prasad note

sections.title: What food means here—and what is still unknown
sections.text: The evidence shows food in different roles: ritual grain in a historical South Indian account, reported prasad after teacher-honouring events in Odisha, and an announced cooked-prasad distribution at a Bhubaneswar institution. These roles should not be collapsed into one festival menu. The Odisha dishes, preparation, household fasting rules and relationship to Dash’s Pausa brata remain unverified.

sections.title: For seasonal visitors
sections.text: Read this as a route into teacher-disciple culture and shared devotional food. A willing institution can explain its own observance, but an old event report or calendar is not a current invitation. Confirm the next local date, access and any prasad arrangement directly before travel. No bookable host or present food service is verified.

pages.name: Shiva Pradosha Brata
pages.traditional_month: Recurring trayodashi in both lunar fortnights; local timing unresolved
pages.lead: A recurring vow makes room for worship within the ordinary month. Shiva Pradosha Brata links restraint from food with devotion to Shiva. Its textual story also makes hunger and care visible through a widow raising two children. For Odisha, the named observance is documented, but a household story tradition and a distinctive local menu still need evidence.

sections.title: A recurring observance in the Odisha account
sections.text: Mahanti describes Shiva Pradosha on trayodashi, the thirteenth lunar day, in both fortnights of each month. He records fasting, Shiva worship, a night vigil and mantra recitation. His paragraph also connects the Phalguna observance with Maha Shivaratri. This is an author’s account of practice; his assertion that few now observe it is not a measured finding about Odisha today.
sections.locator: Printed44/PDF60

sections.title: Evening, sunset or moonrise?
sections.text: Mahanti’s printed page defines a period around moonrise and associates it with the transition from dwadashi to trayodashi. The translated Skanda Purana instead calls Pradosha dusk on the thirteenth day; its procedure places bathing three ghatis before sunset. These descriptions are retained separately. No local worship time is calculated from them.
sections.locator: Mahanti printed44/PDF60, visually checked; Skanda 6.5 and 7.2

sections.title: The widow and the orphaned prince
sections.text: In chapter 6, King Satyaratha dies in war. His queen gives birth while fleeing and is killed by a crocodile. A widow named Uma finds the orphan and, encouraged by Shiva in a mendicant’s form, raises him alongside her own son through alms. The sage Shandilya later teaches them Shiva worship. The chapter frames Pradosha as a time when Shiva dances and the gods gather. This is a religious narrative, not a dated account of Odisha’s past.
sections.locator: Chapter6, verses6–8,16–75 and76–79

sections.title: How the story ends
sections.text: Chapter 7 names the boys Sucivrata and Dharmagupta. After worship, Sucivrata finds treasure. Dharmagupta later marries the Gandharva daughter Amsumati, receives her father’s support and recovers his kingdom. The widow remains his mother and her son his brother. The narrative presents these changes as Shiva’s favour.
sections.locator: Chapter7, verses78–96 and97–159

sections.title: Textual offerings, without an Odisha recipe
sections.text: The translated procedure lists milk pudding, ghee, sweet preparations, sugar and jaggery among offerings; it also directs feeding Brahmins. It allows worship according to one’s means, even with a flower. These are prescriptions in the comparative text, not a verified Odisha menu. Its translated term “cooked pie” is not identified here with any named Odia pitha.
sections.locator: Chapter7, verses52–56 and71

sections.title: Food, care and the limits of interpretation
sections.text: Read together, restraint, offerings and the widow’s care suggest questions about how devotion and feeding others meet. That is an editorial reading, not a claim that all households understand the vow alike. The story’s explanations of poverty and promised rewards belong to its religious framework; they do not establish causes of real hardship or guaranteed benefits from fasting.

sections.title: What the history and food evidence cannot yet tell us
sections.text: No composition date for these chapters, earliest Odisha observance, dated Odia Pradosha katha or named local household account was established in this pass. The translation is a comparison, not proof that the same story was recited locally. Mahanti’s paragraph names fasting but supplies neither a dish nor a fast-breaking recipe. Food from the separate annual Shibaratri profile is not transferred to this recurring vow.

sections.title: For visitors following the ritual year
sections.text: This recurring lunar observance does not by itself define a seasonal food trail. Use the profile to ask a willing local host about their own calendar, story and food roles. A household invitation, temple access, next date and any public serving arrangement all need direct confirmation. No current serving venue or visitor arrangement is verified.

pages.name: Tarini Brata
pages.traditional_month: Ashadha, shukla chaturthi in Mahanti; local annual date unverified
pages.observance_type: regional Shakti brata / household vow distinct from shrine festivals
pages.lead: Tarini Brata brings a hope of protection into the ritual year. Its food story needs several separate strands: fasting in the vow, coconut offerings at Ghatagaon, cooked temple offerings and a coconut sweet associated with the surrounding area. Evidence for one strand does not automatically establish the others.

sections.title: The vow named in an Odisha account
sections.text: Mahanti places Tarini Brata on Ashadha’s bright fourth lunar day. He describes women fasting and worshipping the goddess, with some tying a red thread on the arm, in the hope of relief from difficulties. He locates the observance around Tarini shrines and names Ghatagaon in Keonjhar as the principal shrine. This description gives neither a complete katha nor a food or fast-breaking menu.
sections.locator: Printed46/PDF62

sections.title: Keep three identities distinct
sections.text: The Tarini vow named here is not automatically an alias for Bipattarini. Nor is it the Tara-Tarini yatra that Mahanti separately describes on Chaitra Tuesdays at the hill shrine near the Rushikulya in Ganjam. Names, deities, locality and calendar must be matched before stories or food rules are joined.
sections.locator: Printed46/PDF62 and printed158/PDF174; Bipattarini comparison retained in its existing profile

sections.title: The story of the backward glance
sections.text: Mallebrein records a shrine legend in which Tarini agrees to follow Gobinda Bhanja from Puri provided he never looks back. When her bells fall silent at Ghatagaon, he turns; she becomes stone and stays there. This is an attributed shrine narrative, not a recovered household brata-katha.
sections.locator: Printed158–159, Kanchi-war narrative; author-copy text

sections.title: Dating the shrine is not dating the vow
sections.text: The paper questions the royal chronology behind the familiar 1480 story, citing a tentative seventeenth-century alternative in Senapati’s district history. Neither date establishes the beginning of Tarini Brata. The cited historical work was not independently inspected here.
sections.locator: Printed162–164, historical discussion and note23; claim limited to author’s reported comparison

sections.title: Coconut as an offering
sections.text: Kendujhar’s official district page describes devotees offering coconuts to Tarini at Ghatagaon. That supports a shrine-offering association. It does not identify the food of Ashadha’s household vow or show what visitors can obtain today.
sections.locator: Culture & Heritage introduction, coconut sentence

sections.title: A historical food change with two starting years
sections.text: Mallebrein’s 2004 paper, based on 2002 fieldwork, reports the introduction of cooked anna bhoga and prasad distribution after an earlier fruit-and-coconut practice. It gives 1978 on printed 157 but 1975 on printed 158. Both readings remain unresolved; no single starting year is adopted.
sections.locator: Printed157–158; fieldwork year in printed164 note1

sections.title: Nadia kora belongs to the place evidence
sections.text: The same study associates Ghatagaon with nadia kora, a coconut sweet. This is historical place-food evidence, not a verified Tarini Brata dish, complete recipe or present shop recommendation.
sections.locator: Printed158, coconut distribution and local sweet paragraph

sections.title: Why these distinctions matter
sections.text: Food can be withheld during a vow, offered to a deity, distributed as prasad or sold as a local sweet. Those roles tell different stories about care, devotion and livelihoods. Joining them too quickly would manufacture a festival menu. Here the household vow and shrine food practices remain connected questions, with each source’s setting visible.

sections.title: What remains to be recovered
sections.text: A dated Odia Tarini brata-katha, its edition or manuscript witness, a named locality’s ritual calendar and household preparation remain missing. An online page titled Maa Tarini Brata Katha repeats the saved Mahanti description, mixes in Tara-Tarini material and states that the PDF is unavailable; its title and ten-page label do not establish a recovered text. The original study’s page images and the underlying temple records are also needed to resolve its conflicting food dates.

sections.title: For visitors exploring food and faith
sections.text: Treat Ghatagaon as a place to investigate the relationship between offerings, prasad and local sweets, with a willing local guide or host. Confirm dates, access and any food arrangement directly before travel. No shop, meal service, household invitation or annual Brata date has been verified for visitors. Coconut offerings do not by themselves create a seasonal tasting itinerary.

pages.name: Bajra Mahakali Brata
pages.traditional_month: Aswina amabasya in Mahanti and the inspected Odia story; local annual date unverified
pages.observance_type: brata / Kali household vow; Phuleri and Polari names in the inspected text
pages.lead: In the Bajra Mahakali story, a household prepares an offering while a young daughter-in-law makes a small, consequential mistake: she tastes two grains of rice. Food becomes the thread connecting fear, a difficult promise, separation and a return home. The recovered Odia text also remembers work around the kitchen and the sharing of prasad beyond the family.

sections.title: The observance in a published Odisha account
sections.text: Mahanti places Bajra Mahakali Brata on Aswina amabasya. He describes married women fasting, preparing the household space, offering varieties of pitha to Kali and listening to the brata-katha. Hopes for children are part of his account of devotion, not evidence of a fertility effect. His statement that few people now observe the vow has no stated survey denominator and is not adopted as a current prevalence measure.
sections.locator: Printed49/PDF65

sections.title: A promise made beside the rice
sections.text: The inspected story opens in a prosperous sadhaba, or merchant, household with seven sons and seven daughters-in-law. As the women prepare for the goddess’s worship, the youngest daughter-in-law tastes two grains of soaked rice. Bajra Mahakali confronts her for tasting the unoffered food. Afraid her mother-in-law will hear, she promises the goddess her future sons. The narrative’s accusation and punishment belong to its ritual world; they are not a judgment on women today.
sections.locator: PDF2–3

sections.title: The loss and the return
sections.text: The goddess takes six sons in succession. During the seventh pregnancy, the mother-in-law drives the young woman out on the observance day. In the rain and darkness, the goddess meets her as an old woman, hears her suffering and shelters her. After the seventh birth, she returns the six earlier sons too. The mother comes home with all seven children and explains what happened. The ending presents continued observance as the outcome of the goddess’s test and mercy. These are events within the katha, not verified historical events.
sections.locator: PDF6–11

sections.title: What the kitchen passages actually say
sections.text: The women soak rice and biri, and the rice is to be pounded into flour. A preparation called aradra in the transcription is cooked in a handi; at first it fails to cook, then succeeds after the daughter-in-law appeals to the goddess. The text does not provide ingredient proportions, the complete method or enough detail to identify this preparation with a familiar modern pitha. That identification remains an open food-history question.
sections.locator: PDF3–4; aradra spelling compared with Wikisource transcription

sections.title: Offerings and food shared with neighbours
sections.text: The worship scene places aradra on seven pumpkin leaves. It names banana, coconut and a preparation of seven kinds of greens, without naming the greens individually. It also uses the categories nishankhudi and shankhudi; their precise contents here require local explanation. After the worship and story, the prasad is shared among those present and given to neighbours. Plants and branches arranged for worship are recorded separately from edible dishes; their presence does not make every plant an ingredient.
sections.locator: PDF5

sections.title: Names and dates need their own evidence
sections.text: The title pairs Bajra Mahakali Brata with Phuleri Osha, while the body uses Polari/Polori forms and names Aswina amabasya. This supports an association within this particular text, not a universal equivalence with every similarly named Pithori observance elsewhere. No Gregorian date or named locality’s present calendar has been verified.
sections.locator: PDF1–2,7,10–11; Mahanti printed49/PDF65

sections.title: History: a recovered witness with an undated imprint
sections.text: Project Pothi’s repository credits Prateek Pattanaik with providing and scanning the booklet and records its upload in2017. Its description gives a1934 date and claims a sixteenth-century or sixteenth-to-seventeenth-century author, but the supplied pages show no original imprint establishing these claims. The anonymous scan is a recoverable textual witness; neither the composition date nor the beginning of the observance is established. Its merchant-family setting alone is not evidence of an overseas-trade origin.
sections.locator: Commons description/date/author and file-history fields; all11 PDF pages inspected for imprint

sections.title: Significance: household labour and belonging
sections.text: Read as a story, the katha brings a young woman’s vulnerability into the same space as ritual discipline, cooking and family authority. The reunion changes the course of blame and exclusion. The food scene adds a social dimension: offerings become something the family and neighbours share. This is an editorial interpretation of one narrative, not a claim that all participants explain the vow this way. A future account from willing local practitioners should be allowed to differ.

sections.title: For a seasonal food journey
sections.text: The text provides questions for a guide or food researcher: what is aradra called locally, which greens are used, who prepares the offering, and how is it shared? It does not verify a tasting venue, public invitation, purchasable meal or current household practice. Keep the food association visible, and confirm a willing host and local date before planning an encounter.

pages.name: Mahastami Brata
pages.traditional_month: Aswina bright-fortnight eighth day during autumn Durga Puja
pages.observance_type: household Durga brata within the autumn festival; relationship to regional Durgastami names unresolved
pages.lead: Mahastami brings the household vow into the wider season of Durga worship. Its short published account places fruit, fasting and a brata worn after worship at the centre. Understanding that small ritual scene also requires asking which story a household reads and how its food differs from the neighbouring traditions of Bhai Jiuntia and public Durga Puja.

sections.title: The household account
sections.text: Mahanti places Mahastami Brata on Aswina’s bright eighth day. Married women fast, worship a brata before Durga with fruit, then wear it; he also mentions reading Durgastami brata-katha. He supplies neither named fruit varieties nor a complete story.
sections.locator: Printed51/PDF67, Mahastami brata paragraph

sections.title: A festival meal is a separate food setting
sections.text: In his wider Durga Puja chapter, Mahanti describes devotees bringing bhoga for offering and eating after pushpanjali and arati. This is a public-festival description. It does not establish the household vow’s fast-breaking time, exact dishes or a menu shared by every locality.

sections.title: Why the names need comparison
sections.text: One seller lists a22-page Odia booklet titled Bhai Jiuntia Osha Katha ba Durgastami Brata o Durgashrimala, attributed to Dharma Grantha Store, Cuttack. That linked title is a useful lead for comparing names. The book’s contents and imprint have not been recovered, so it cannot yet establish that every Mahastami household follows the same katha as Bhai Jiuntia.
sections.locator: Product title and Specifications, item HAR390

sections.title: What can be narrated, and where it belongs
sections.text: The saved Bhai Jiuntia study now supplies a short, attributed Malathi and Mathana Kumar narrative and an account of group recitation. Read it on the linked Bhai Jiuntia page in its western Odisha setting. Transferring that story to this household entry would require the actual Durgastami text or situated evidence of its use. No complete Mahastami katha is narrated here.

sections.title: History still to establish
sections.text: A present-day catalogue entry cannot date a story’s composition or the beginning of a vow. The next historical step is to recover an identifiable edition, inspect its imprint and narrative, and compare it with dated manuscripts and situated accounts. A shared lunar day or deity alone cannot demonstrate one origin.

sections.title: Significance through household practice
sections.text: The account invites a reading of devotion as preparation, restraint, storytelling and something carried on the body after worship. Food has several possible roles: an offering, something shared, and a meal that ends a fast. Keeping those roles separate makes space for households to explain their own practice. This is an editorial interpretation and a research agenda, not a claim that all participants give the vow one meaning.

sections.title: For a seasonal food journey
sections.text: Use the autumn lunar season as a reading and enquiry cue. Ask a willing local host which name they use, what is offered, what is eaten afterwards and whether visitors are welcome. Fruit in an account does not establish a special dish sold nearby; a public festival does not establish access to a private household. No current Gregorian date, serving venue or host arrangement has been verified.

pages.name: Ashoka Astami Brata
pages.traditional_month: Chaitra bright-fortnight eighth; textual bud prescription additionally specifies Punarvasu
pages.observance_type: household Surya brata in Mahanti; distinct textual and Rukuna Ratha comparisons
pages.lead: Ashoka Astami opens three related but different lines of enquiry: a household vow for children, a prayer involving spring flower buds, and Bhubaneswar’s Rukuna Ratha festival. Their shared name invites comparison. It does not yet establish one story, one deity or one meal across all three.

sections.title: A household vow to Surya
sections.text: Mahanti describes married women observing a Chaitra bright-eighth vow to Surya for their children’s well-being. His brief entry names no food or household katha. He also says the vow is no longer observed, but gives no survey or locality-level evidence for that conclusion; its present prevalence remains unknown.
sections.locator: Printed53/PDF69, Ashoka ashtami brata

sections.title: Rama and the festival story
sections.text: In Mahanti’s separate festival account, Ravana is protected by Durga. Following Vibhishana’s advice, Rama worships her; she withdraws her support on the eighth day. Rama defeats Ravana and celebrates with a chariot procession of Shiva and Durga. This is the author’s attributed legend, not a dated founding event or a recovered story of the household Surya vow.
sections.locator: Printed107–108/PDF123–124, Ashoka astami puja

sections.title: The public procession as a separate setting
sections.text: Incredible India places Asokastami at Lingaraja in Bhubaneswar and describes the Rukuna Ratha procession to Rameswara Temple. Its Rama-origin account is presented here as mythology. The page’s general invitation to experience local gastronomy names neither an observance-specific dish nor a verified serving place.
sections.locator: Historical Roots and Celebratory Myths; The Spectacle of the Rukuna Rath Yatra; Engaging in the Festivities

sections.title: Eight buds in a textual prescription
sections.text: The opening of chapter CXXXIII in the Garuda Purana translation attributed to Manmatha Nath Dutt prescribes eating eight ashoka flower buds on Chaitra’s bright eighth when joined with Punarvasu. Its prayer addresses ashoka as dear to Hara and seeks release from grief. This is a ritual prescription and promise within the text, not evidence of a health effect.
sections.locator: Chapter CXXXIII opening paragraph, before Mahanavami

sections.title: What this adds to food history
sections.text: The bud passage records ritual consumption rather than a complete cooked meal. It does not identify the household Surya vow’s offerings, a fast-breaking dish, an Odisha recipe or a present serving custom. Nothing in the inspected passage supplies curd or a preparation method. The text is recorded for cultural comparison, not as a foraging or eating recommendation.

sections.title: History: distinguish witnesses from origins
sections.text: The digital host labels Dutt’s translation1908; that bibliographic attribution does not date the Sanskrit passage, its arrival in Odisha or the beginning of the household vow. A dated local text, a securely identified edition and situated accounts are needed to connect the three settings historically. Mahanti’s compilation and a tourism retelling cannot establish uninterrupted continuity.

sections.title: Significance: care and the wish to lose sorrow
sections.text: Concern for children, the textual prayer against grief and the festival’s story of recovery offer different ways to explore care and hope. This is an editorial comparison. It leaves room for participants to explain their own meanings rather than fitting every practice into one origin story. In food research, the most useful next question is what each community actually offers, shares and eats.

sections.title: For a seasonal visitor
sections.text: Treat Chaitra as a traditional calendar label requiring a year-specific local check. The public procession and household vow need separate access information. No current date, food seller, tasting arrangement or consenting household host has been established. The named flower in a religious text must not be turned into a visitor menu.

food_names: Eight ashoka flower buds — comparative textual prescription only; Odisha household menu unverified
questions: Can an original Odia household katha or dated witness identify the Surya vow and its transmission?
What evidence supports continuity, change or non-observance in named localities?
Can an identifiable print edition and Sanskrit passage verify the digital Garuda Purana transcription?
Does an inspected Balarama Dasa Ramayana passage connect Sita and ashoka buds, as a later article suggests?
What foods are offered, shared and eaten in each household or temple setting, with recipes and local names?
Can a current authoritative schedule and willing host establish a specific visitor opportunity?

pages.name: Raja Parba
pages.traditional_month: Mithuna Sankranti; solar transition described as Jyestha to Ashadha in Mohapatra
pages.observance_type: agrarian and social parba; included alongside household osha and brata
pages.lead: Raja can be read through a household kitchen as well as a swing. Food made ahead, time away from everyday work, visits to relatives and portions of pitha sent between homes bring the season into social life. The festival connects the coming rains with a belief in the Earth’s menstrual rest; its foods help tell how that rest is imagined and organised.

sections.title: The Earth at rest
sections.text: In Mahanti’s account, Basumati or Bhu-devi is believed to menstruate for three days as the rainy season approaches. Cultivation pauses, and a fourth-day Basumati snana marks renewal. This is the festival’s sacred explanation, not a literal account of the soil or a dated event in its origin. The author places particular emphasis on Cuttack and surrounding districts; the account does not establish a uniform custom across Odisha.
sections.locator: Printed116–117 / PDF132–133, Raja parba

sections.title: A calendar organised around Sankranti
sections.text: Mohapatra’s June 2006 article describes Pahili Raja at the end of Jyestha, Raja or Mithuna Sankranti at the start of Ashadha, and Bhuin Dahana on the following day. It notes a fourth-day Basumata Puja in some places. These are traditional calendar descriptions, not a fixed Gregorian itinerary. Mahanti uses Basi Raja for the third day and gives a solar Mithuna/lunar Jyestha description. Preserve the calendar systems and names rather than silently treating every month label as interchangeable.
sections.locator: Mohapatra printed122 / PDF1; Mahanti printed116–117 / PDF132–133

sections.title: Preparing food before the pause
sections.text: Mahanti connects the suspension of cutting, grinding and cooking with food prepared in advance, naming podo pitha, arisha and muan. He also describes pitha exchanged between relatives and neighbours. Read together, these passages make the kitchen central to the festival: a period of rest relies on work already done, and a cake can become a gift between households. That connection is an editorial reading of his description, not a measured account of who performs the preparatory labour today. His claim that these foods remain unspoilt for several days is not adopted as storage advice.
sections.locator: Printed117–119 / PDF133–135

sections.title: Poda pitha, arisa and the wider festive meal
sections.text: The saved Odisha Tourism description presents poda pitha as slowly cooked fermented rice batter, using sal leaves and an earthen pot. The saved ICAR-CRRI compilation describes arisa made from rice flour with jaggery or sugar syrup, shaped and fried. These are separately attributed institutional preparation summaries, not standardised household recipes. Mohapatra lists rice powder, molasses, coconut and ghee among poda-pitha ingredients and describes cakes being shared; he gives no reproducible recipe. The saved June 2026 Akashvani report also names poda and arisa in Raja celebrations. Together these records support the association while leaving proportions, cooking vessels, fillings and household versions open.
sections.locator: Tourism Poda Pitha heading; ICAR-CRRI printed9 / PDF20, Arisa; Mohapatra printed123 / PDF2; Akashvani15June2026 third body paragraph

sections.title: Swings, songs and visiting
sections.text: Mahanti describes swings hung from mango or banyan trees, groups singing Raja ballads, puchi games and visits among friends and relations. Food sharing belongs to this setting of sociability. His recollection of improvised footwear made from areca-palm material is a remembered detail, not a date for the festival’s beginning. The account’s general claim that Raja is fading has no supporting survey here; the later food-service and news records likewise cannot measure whether participation is growing or declining.
sections.locator: Printed117–119 / PDF133–135; footnote53

sections.title: Rest, pleasure and restrictions
sections.text: Raja’s imagery offers a way to discuss the value attached to the Earth, girls’ social lives and respite from routine labour. The same descriptions record limits on movement, washing and household work and frame girlhood through future marriage. A careful narrative can acknowledge pleasure and restrictions together. It should not claim that every participant experiences empowerment, stigma or rest in the same way. Situated accounts from women of different ages and communities are still needed.

sections.title: A documented change in food distribution
sections.text: An official July 2021 tourism newsletter reports OTDC’s Pitha-on-Wheels during pandemic restrictions, with takeaway sales scheduled for 14–16 June 2021. The programme named poda pitha, manda, kakara, arisa, chakuli and chandrakala and six pickup areas in Bhubaneswar. It offers a dated example of public provision of festival food alongside household preparation. It does not establish when commercial Raja cooking began, that every outlet stocked every dish, or what is available now.
sections.locator: Odisha Unravelled July2021 issue8, printed8 / PDF8

sections.title: What the historical record establishes
sections.text: The 2006 article is a dated witness to a published description of Raja. The undated Mahanti compilation adds remembered and narrated practices; the 2021 programme and 2026 report provide later dated records. This sequence is a history of the evidence inspected, not a continuous history of the festival. No securely dated first observance, founding dynasty or earliest literary passage has been established. Similar descriptions in two publications do not prove independent testimony.

sections.title: Looking for Raja food as a visitor
sections.text: Use the June seasonal association to begin an enquiry, then check the intended year and place. Poda pitha and arisa are useful foods to ask about; a historical programme’s wider menu is not a current offer. Before recommending a visit, establish the serving date, named operator, menu, price and access. Household cooking is a private setting unless a host has agreed to receive visitors. No current seller or household invitation has been verified for this profile.

food_names: muan — Mahanti’s named preparation; recipe unresolved
questions: Can dated Odia literature, gazetteers or archival descriptions establish earlier Raja witnesses without mistaking a literary reference for an origin date?
Can the museum-hosted Rajo, The Swing Festival of Kalinga (India) be recovered with its issue, byline, references and historical claims checked?
How do names, cooking schedules and foods vary by locality, community and household?
Who does the work before and during the festival, and how do participants describe rest and restrictions in their own terms?
Which dated public offers actually name foods, prices and visitor access for the intended year?
